If they ever did that, I just hope they do weight balancing better because the superstrike is pretty front heavy, but I'm perfectly happy with Razer's optical switches because they just feel sooooo good. But I think the haptic analog switches would be very interesting in the Deathadder shape. I really don't know how they could improve on this other than finding more ways to lighten the weight even more. Razer might've perfected the Viper with this iteration.

This is the best gaming mouse as someone who upgraded from a regular stock mouse. The weight, the functionality, and the design of the mouse is perfect. In fact, this mouse, and it features had further fine-tuned my already decent aim. After using this mouse for a while, I have observed my aim became a natural aim bot, where I was even accused of potentially exploiting in a match of BF1. The mouse itself is light, and as someone who came from a heavier mouse it felt a bit weird at first. However, if you can manage it, then it becomes a benefit. It allows you to flick quickly, and track targets consistently, which is where my claim of "natural aim bot" came from. It's not too light where you might find yourself tensing up too much to keep it in place, but if you came from a heavier mouse, then you might overflick your target a few times. The features the mouse offered through Razer's Synapse software such as the DPI and mappings are very useful. You can set different profiles for different games, so there are different DPI's for each game. In addition, you can change the mouse's buttons to be mapped to keys on your keyboard. For example, you can have the side button mapped to 'R', so you can reload through the side button. You can also have the same side buttons run a macro, so if you're playing Helldivers 2, you can instantly input a stratagem through your side button. There are also features like letting the side buttons launch a program. The mouse also features polling rates up to 8k, where higher rates increases the consistency of your cursor's tracking across the screen, and decreases latency. HOWEVER, higher rates can drain the battery life faster, and require specific hardware. Increased polling rates will put higher loads onto your CPU, so ensure you have a strong enough CPU. Otherwise, CPU intensive games will suffer FPS drops, or in general, some games might have issues or do not even support said polling rates. In addition, to notice the different in polling rates, a monitor with a higher refresh rate will be required. Regardless, using 2k and 4k, I haven't really noticed a difference as someone who has a 180hz monitor. It feels the same as 1k polling rate, but if you have the hardware to support it, use it! Regarding the battery life, it's very very good. I have used 2k and 4k polling rates for hours in a day, and the battery only goes down from 100% to like 96%. Whereas if you use 1k polling rate, then the battery doesn't even drain at all till the next day or two maybe (I charge it overnight once the day ends). Upgrading from a wired mouse, and as someone who was a firm believer that wired mice was better, this mouse changed that. I found the wireless mode of this mouse more consistent, than my wired mouse, and offered more freedom in wrist/arm movement. Therefore, I was able to track better. Also, the latency was small on it, perhaps even better. However, you can use the USB cable and plug it into the mouse if you'd like to use it wired. The design of the mouse is comfortable for those who use a claw grip. I typically have my palm touching the mouse, and my fingers in a claw like stance on it. I found no discomfort, and was able to consistently aim. As for other grips, I do not know. If you're upgrading from a stock mouse, then this is worth the upgrade. However, please read other reviews, if you're upgrading from like Razer's Viper V3 Pro mouse, then it might not be worth the money. Since the V3 shares many similarities to the V4 with a few new features. Overall, this might be one of the best mice on the market right now. This mouse ended up being the final piece in the puzzle for me towards perfect aim. Somehow, my peripherals were holding me back, where it is typically the opposite.

I don’t typically write reviews, but this mouse is hands down the best I’ve ever had the pleasure of using, so I feel like I must. The moment my hand gripped the mouse, I knew it was the one. The build quality is fantastic. Everything. From the clicks to the sensor, the scroll wheel and the side buttons. Everything is perfect. The coating on the mouse is high quality and the dongle that comes with it is nicely weighted so it doesn’t slip around on your desk. The stock skates are also wonderful and glide around on my Artisan Zero Soft so smoothly. The size and shape is perfect for my grip style (relaxed claw) so I can handle it comfortably. I recently just bought a GPX Superlight 2 as well as an X2 Crazylight Medium and neither felt quite right. So I decided to try this mouse and it did everything for me the other two couldn’t. Since I bought the Razer Viper V4 Pro, I’ve seen a massive improvement in my gameplay. And for that reason I can confidently justify the price of this product. 5 Stars. Genuinely amazing product across the board. Dare I say perfect. 👍 ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

review_title: Left me Surprised in a Good Way
body_en: This mouse took me by surprise. Coming from the Basilisk V3 Pro, this one is just so lightweight that I almost mistook it for a toy. I seriously can't believe how light this is. The battery life is phenomenal, and the controls are astoundingly tight. The buttons on my Basilisk always felt cheap and mushy, but every button on this Viper V4 Pro is snappy and solid. Getting to the part people care about most, this is probably the most fluid mouse I've ever used. The 50K sensor is a marketing ploy, as I don't use anything over 6400DPI, but you can turn on the 8K polling with a high refresh rate monitor and you won't see any dragging of your cursor across your screen as you will with lower refresh rates, and the higher polling rate shows your mouse's location on the screen more times per second than traditional 1K polling rates. My eyes can see the difference, but only if I strain to see it. I run the mouse at 1K polling rate for optimal battery life and because most games are using that rate the most effectively. It's a sweet spot. So the reasons to get the mouse are simple: lightweight, long battery life, no skipping, truly ambidextrous. The cons: no wireless charging, and no RGB. But those are apparent tradeoffs for that impossibly light 49 gram feel.

The Razer Viper V4 Pro is a flagship-level esports mouse that doubles down on performance rather than reinventing the formula. It features an ultra-lightweight ambidextrous design at around 49–50g, paired with Razer’s Focus Pro 50K optical sensor capable of 50,000 DPI, 930 IPS tracking, and 90G acceleration. It also introduces Gen-4 optical switches, improved wireless performance with an upgraded dongle, and up to 180 hours of battery life. On paper, it’s one of the most technically refined mice available fast, consistent, and clearly built for competitive play. That said, if you already own the Razer Viper V3 Pro, there’s honestly no real reason to upgrade. The improvements here are incremental slightly better battery life, marginally upgraded switches, and small refinements that you’re not going to feel in-game. The V3 Pro is already insanely lightweight, responsive, and accurate, so the V4 Pro ends up feeling more like a spec bump than a meaningful evolution. Unless you’re chasing absolute top-end specs for the sake of it, you’re better off sticking with the V3 Pro. As a stand alone mouse, I give it 4 stars. As a "upgrade" to the previous generation I'd give it one star.

review_title: New main. Excellent mouse with a ridiculous battery life
body_en: The box didn't have much protection, but it arrived in great condition. As for the mouse itself, it is amazing. I won't talk much about shape because that's highly subjective (I'll just say it fits my hand size and grip style), but everything else is excellent: coating is smooth and grippy, very nice to the touch; main clicks are light and tactile, tho they could have a little less post travel; side buttons are well tensioned and positioned; the wheel might be the weakest aspect, because the scrolling feels a bit off, but it's totally functional; M3 click is very tactile; skates are smooth and fast; build quality is perfect, solid as a rock; performance is top tier, no complaints; and finally, the battery is absolutely insane. I have been using the mouse for 12 days at 1000hz (sometimes 8000, but only for a couple of Apex matches) and it has only gone down to 60%. On top of all of that, Razer has finally made a web software. That means 2 things: 1) you don't have to deal with the bloatware that is Synapse (except for firmware updates); and 2) you can change your settings on Linux, which has been a game changer for me (I dual boot Windows 11 and Bazzite). I think it is worth the price, but only if you don't have a Viper V3 Pro (or even a Viper V3 Pro SE). On paper, the V4 Pro has many improvements, but the only real upgrade that a player will notice is the battery life and the web software. I recommend it to people who have never owned a Viper V3 and want the latest technology and power efficiency. I can recommend it to those who just want to try the shape, but they might also want to take a look at the V3 Pro, since it is cheaper right now.

I have been using it a full week now, and I think it's worth all the praise. It's a safe shape that will work for everyone except if your hands are on the smaller side. Switches, side buttons, scroll wheel, and sensor all feel perfect. My honest favorite thing about this mouse is the battery life is otherworldly good compared to anything I have used. I likely won't have to charge it until about 5-6 weeks of moderate to heavy use at 1000Hz, which is huge when I need to charge my other mice practically after a weekend. The first negative is the price is steep, especially when you could get the V3 Pro Se for like have the price. Two, the M1/M2 switches are on the loud side, but you won't notice them with headphones. You will annoy anyone around you though if they have to listen to you click. Three, the black version is a bit of an oil magnet, but the coating at least feels good. Might be worth using either Razer's provided grips or another brands for long-term use. Overall, it's a very good mouse if it's within your price range, and your hands are moderately large in size. Maybe it's placebo, but I also dropped my first nuke in Call of Duty on keyboard and mouse using it. That might be influencing might personal opinion of it, but I promise it's a great mouse.

review_title: G502 X Plus -- A Worthy successor to earlier G502's for FPS games
body_en: The 2022 Logitech G502 X Plus was a very pleasant surprise. It is replacing a Logitech G-Pro that is roughly 80 grams weight on a Logitech Powerplay mouse pad (expanded cover for extra space and non-stop charging), primarily used for Overwatch2. Other gaming mice in my collection include earlier G502's, G903, Razer Death Adder + Copperhead, Steelseries Rival3 and Rival600, etc. Generally the best performers in FPS games are the lightest units with the best optical sensors, and the G502 X Plus definitely fits that criteria. Pros: -Comfortable ergonomic shape for marathon gaming sessions -PTFE mouse feet for super-smooth glide across mouse pads -The new optical hybrid switches are incredibly fast compared to the G-Pro's older Omron switches, with a nice crisp click and improved actuation. They will last much longer than conventional mechanical switches and correct double-clicking issues. My last G-Pro's right rear thumb switch suffered from double-clicking issues since they were the old Omron mechanicals that wore out from constant use. -Nice RGB lighting if you are looking for that kind of bling -This mouse wakes from sleep mode instantly (like the G-Pro series). The old G502 Hero Wireless required a full second to wake up, making the old sleep mode feature extremely inconvenient and annoying. -At 106 grams list weight, the G502 X Plus is a tad heavier for a gaming mouse. However, coming from an 80 gram G-Pro, I notice better aim stability without sacrificing flick aim consistency. With the Powerplay charging puck attached and USB receiver stored inside, the G502 X Plus hits 110g on my postal scale. The G502 Hero wireless is 120g with the same accessories. Cons: -No more adjustable weights like its predecessor G502, but to be fair, the whole e-sport industry has shifted competitive user demand to lighter weight mice for the fastest aim flicks possible. -Battery power drains faster with RGB lighting at full settings. This is mitigated by reducing RBG brightness to 85% and shortening idle-mode entry from 2 minutes down to 1. Using a Logitech Powerplay mouse pad, my mouse battery power hovers around 78% to 90% steady with RGB enabled. -The mouse's black finish tends to have shiny oil stains and wear marks over time. This is why I apply blue painter's tape to the areas most prone to this issue. EDIT Feb 2024 - I've replaced the blue painter's tape with automotive carbon fiber vinyl wrap for better visual appeal. Not recommended if you do not like the feel of textured carbon fiber, but it definitely gets rid of those shiny oil stains. Picture attached. -GHub software will not allow users less than 3 DPI presets, and all of these have to be different values at 50dpi intervals. I tried to "lock" my mouse at 1000dpi to avoid accidental DPI switching, but the software would not allow me to do this, so I ended up moving my DPI cycling button to the default profile button up top and removing the up/down DPI adjustment buttons next to the left click. This gave me two additional buttons for other programable functions (like Alt and middle-mouse click since pressing the mouse wheel down can feel awkward). EDIT -- GHUB finally fixed this issue. I can now run with just 1000dpi single setting. -The new hybrid mechanical switches have a different click sound compared to conventional switches -- not really louder, but definitely more metallic. Yes, this mouse is expensive, but the combination of lighter weight + excellent ergonomics + fast/crisp long-wear switches makes this model very hard to beat. If you are looking for a mouse with more weight and heft, then you may not be happy with the G502 X since the latest model has been redesigned for the e-sports crowd. The G502 X now combines lighter weight with an ergo shape, something that most ultra-light mouse offerings lack. NOTE: If you want the best wireless mouse experience, I recommend pairing the G502 X Plus with a Logitech Powerplay for non-stop wireless charging while using the mouse. For those that want a larger mouse pad than what the default Powerplay size offers, check out "Logitech powerplay mousepad expansion mod" on youtube. I have my set-up displayed in the attached images along with actual weight compared to the old G502 Wireless. Update 4/26/2023: The Glorious XL mousepad is the perfect thickness for this Powerplay expansion mod. EDIT: I just read a few other reviews claiming that the G502 X feels "cheap" because it feels too light. The whole point of lowering mouse weight is to minimize mass, thereby requiring less physical energy / effort to move the mouse quickly and accurately. This is how modern e-sports mice are designed, because a lighter mouse is a faster mouse, while a heavier one is a slower boat anchor that is usually on the losing end of an FPS fire fight. The G502 X Plus is only 10 grams lighter than the G502 hero, yet it is much easier to flick-aim than the older G502 Hero Wireless. Also, if you want RGB on the G502 X, you have to get the Plus edition, other wise you get no RGB. Yet one newer review complained about missing RGB LED's on his G502 X non-Plus edition. Going no-RGB is still a valid choice since it saves a few grams, extends battery life, and costs less, but just make sure you know what you are buying ahead of time. ;)

review_title: My New Gaming Sidekick: The Logitech G502 X Plus!
body_en: Alright, let's talk about the new star of my desk setup – the Logitech G502 X Plus Wireless Gaming Mouse. As someone who spends a good chunk of time in front of the PC, this isn't just a peripheral; it's practically an extension of my hand, and honestly, it feels like it was designed specifically for me. First off, the wireless freedom is a game-changer (pun absolutely intended). Ditching the cable is just chef's kiss for decluttering and those intense gaming sessions where every millisecond counts. And the LIGHTSPEED Optical connection? Flawless. There's no perceptible lag, no hiccups, just pure, unadulterated responsiveness. My old M720 Triathlon is still great for everyday use, and it's my go-to when this beast needs a charge, but for serious pixel-peeping and headshot hunting, the G502 X Plus blows it out of the water. The HERO 25K Sensor is no joke. I'm talking pinpoint accuracy that makes navigating my Alienware 38 Curved and 34 QD-OLED monitors feel like butter. Whether I'm trying to land that perfect shot or meticulously editing a document, this mouse tracks like a dream. And the LIGHTFORCE Switches? Every click feels crisp and satisfying, giving you that tactile feedback that just confirms your action. No mushiness here, just pure, responsive clicks. Then there's the LIGHTSYNC RGB. Look, I appreciate a bit of flair, and this mouse delivers without being over the top. It adds that perfect touch of gaming aesthetic, syncing up with the rest of my setup, like my Gimars RGB Gaming Mouse Pad. It just makes the whole experience feel more immersive and, frankly, cooler. This mouse just fits. The ergonomic design feels great in my hand, even during those extended sessions. It's not too light, not too heavy, and the button placement feels intuitive. It's built for comfort and performance, and you can really tell. In short, if you're serious about your PC experience, especially gaming, the Logitech G502 X Plus is an absolute winner. It's fast, accurate, comfortable, and looks damn good doing it. My gaming setup feels complete with this bad boy. Highly recommend it to anyone looking for a top-tier wireless gaming mouse!

review_title: Avoid. The G-Hub software simply does not work.
body_en: Title says it all. I bought 2 of these, figuring I could sync profiles between my desktop and laptop gaming systems. The mouse is mechanically well built, but there are plenty of mice that are mechanically just as good. If you're buying a gaming mouse with all the extra buttons, then you probably play more than one video game... which requires software to change the "profile" or button functions for each different game... and that's where this mouse falls apart. The G-hub software seems designed to do everything Except what you want to do: -You want to change button functions? By Yourself? Gosh, even if you do figure out the interface and psychically intuit that the keys have to be drag/dropped onto the buttons to change them, they still won't change. I mean, why would you need to? We scanned all software on your hard drive and sent the list to our marketing dept, and they auto-set profiles that work great! They promise! -You want to unlock the profile so you can change the button settings? Aw, too bad choom. It's locked because, um, we felt it was necessary to lock the buttons for some reason. Like you might accidentally open this software and accidentally drag/drop functions you didn't really mean to change. Best to leave it locked, for your own good. -You want to change profiles? Oh, sure you can do that. Until you navigate away from G-hub and then it "helps" by auto-changing the profile back to Default! No worries, our marketing team has your back. I mean, they are gaming experts! You should SEE their score on Candy Crush! -You still want to change profiles? Why? I mean, we auto-detect the application for you! Spent a lot of money on that, choom. Why you wanna mess that up? -Want to sync your gaming profiles across two computers? Yeah, we know you tied your G-hub software to your logitech account and thanks so much for that data pipe from your computer to the cloud, but really, our marketing department NEEDS that so they can gather data from your system. You know, to uh... track performance and issues and stuff. We're afraid there just isn't the bandwidth to move your settings to the cloud and over to a whole other device. Sorries, but like we said, our software auto-detects and auto-sets the prefect settinz 4 U! We are soo accurat, and xcelnt qualitee! Promize! So the G-hub software is crap designed by idiots, but don't listen to me. I only have a BA in Computer Science and 24 years experience working in IT, and played video games since Dungeons of Daggorath on the TRS-80. But be my guest and google "Manual for G HUB?" for yourself. Do yourself a favor - buy 3 mice for this price and throw the two worst ones away. You will STILL be money ahead, and have a way better experience. At least until Logitech hires an actual software interface designer.

review_title: Cheap switches you will have to replace. I wish Asus would have done better with this product.
body_en: Here is the deal I have with this mouse: brand new out of the box and already have double-clicking going on. Two weeks of use. While they do include a spare set of switches, this still does not account for the fact they are cheap. No wonder it's designed so one can replace switches so easily. For the price, Asus should be ASHAMED. For me, I just ordered proper switches to replace what this product came with. Not a big deal as they are dirt cheap. But still, as I stated, for a $100+ mouse, the switches should not be this cheap. This is a heavy mouse. If you use a cloth mouse pad, you are not going to like this mouse. You feel the friction and the weight of this mouse on this material. I switched to my Logitech G440 hard-covered mouse pad, and it slides like a dream. I was going to order glass skates. Glad I did not. If you install new states, you will be unable to use the dock mount. I do like the fact that there are 6 side buttons. Using a glass mouse pad or hard cover allows me to play FPS games with ease. I like the 5 DPI settings, but, again, for the price, they could have added a few more possibilities. For a few dollars more, you can have a G502 with superior hardware but a lack of side buttons. I operate in an entire Asus ecosystem; I have an Asus motherboard, PSU, AIO cooler, 5080 GPU, & 3 monitors, so I already have Armory Crate installed on my system. If you buy this mouse, you HAVE to install Armory Crate to make use of this mouse in any good way. That being said, Armory Crate is notorious for being known as bloatware. Which, in my opinion, it is. There's really no need for it to be running and eating up system resources like this app does. So buyer beware. I would have brought a Razer instead, but that mouse too requires that you install their software to work their mouse. The lesser of two evils for me was this mouse. The construction, meaning the mouse shapes and material, feels robust and tank-like. But I dare not drop it. It feels like a smartphone: it looks built for durability and day-to-day use, but one drop and it's broken. Mainly because of the weight of this mouse. It's like dropping a brick from 2'. So take care of your equipment or at least get the protection. I know this review sounds bad, but it's really not. I do enjoy this mouse; I like the fit in my hand (I have mid-size hands), I love the ring finger resting point, and the scroll wheel is smooth. My issues are stated: It should come with better switches; one needs a hard surface area to really be able to move this mouse without muscle failure, and the bloatware just to use this. It should be a $60 mouse, because in the end, you will be buying upgraded switches and looking for a mouse pad that will work well with this mouse. As far as gameplay, it does take some getting used to, but it's doable. Back in the day, gamers used to play FPS with ball mice. While this is 1000% better, a lightweight/gamer mouse would be a better pick. The 6 side buttons are the lifesaver for this mouse for me. While it takes a little time to set up profiles so they do work in the games you are playing, once it's done, you are golden. Windows does not support any more than, like, 3 or 4 side buttons, so you have to program the unsupported ones to bind to keys, then in-game, bind that key to your mouse. All in all, a good, solid mouse as long as you don't mind the 'little' headaches that come along with it. 3 stars because there are better mice out there & for a company like Asus, I would expect better from them. EDIT (PLEASE READ!): I really wanted to love this mouse. The shape and the heavy chassis feel fantastic in the hand, but for the premium price tag, the internal hardware is an absolute nightmare. The biggest issue—and the reason I had to abandon it—is the mechanical microswitches. I bought this in April, and within a few months of normal gaming, it developed a severe double-clicking issue and started dropping window drags. It got to the point where it was actively sabotaging my gameplay; I would press the rear middle side button (which I use for missile lock-ons or grenade throwing), and the switch simply wouldn't register the input. ASUS tries to market their "push-fit hot-swap switch sockets" as a feature, but it's really a band-aid for their use of cheap, outdated mechanical parts. I tried fixing it myself by buying three different sets of replacement mechanical microswitches. None of them held up, and the mouse continued to miss clicks and fail. This proves the issue isn't just the switches themselves, but a fundamental flaw in the PCB, the socket design, or the firmware relying on 1990s-era mechanical contacts. The side buttons are also prone to sticking, even after a thorough cleaning, making them unreliable in crucial gaming moments. Furthermore, you have to deal with Armoury Crate, which is a bloated mess; their own updates ruined the mouse profiles I had set. Did it 3 times, and the constant fear that a speck of dust or a stray cat hair will get inside the chassis and ruin the contacts. If you are a serious gamer looking for a reliable, long-term peripheral, look elsewhere. Do not buy a mouse at this price point that still uses mechanical switches. Save yourself the headache and buy something with modern optical switches (like the Razer Naga V2 Pro or Corsair Scimitar) that physically cannot double-click. Thankfully, Amazon Customer Service was amazing and granted me a one-time return exception because of how quickly this hardware failed. I took that refund and immediately bought a mouse with optical switches.

I could probably look past this if the mouse had enough buttons but can't in this case and is worth mentioning. - Although very minor, this mouse is only 1000Hz versus the 2000-8000Hz that competitors offer. review_title: I don't like Razer, but this mouse slaps

The software took so much finagling and trial and error manually deleting Synapse and re-installing more than once--I even tried deleting Synapse data online from my account via the Privacy Center to no avail. Midway through, I almost just resorted to keeping things on onboard memory and manually switching between games. It was brutal. Thankfully profile switching started working and button remaps followed suit. I don't know how I got it to work, but it works! It handles so well that the pain setting up the software can be forgiven. This is everything I wanted out of my old Logitech G600s, of which I've had several and daily drove for the better part of a decade. I'd always try but ultimately return other MMO mice because I'd always miss ring-finger button. I know I'm not the only one that felt this! It seems like Razer heard our cries and implemented it on this new Naga V3 Pro, even adding the two additional buttons by the left-click button like on the V2 Hyperspeed. My only gripes are that the side buttons aren't as pronounced and contoured as the G600, and the left- and right-mouse clicks are just obnoxiously loud. Travel distance and weight per click as well I'd say aren't great either--maybe better for older MMOs where each click needed to be more deliberate, but a lighter switch would be better for modern MMOs. I guess I'll get used to them. Despite all of that, the fact that in addition to the extra buttons this is wireless AND I can swap plates for other non-MMO games? I can learn to live with this. This review is for the Razer Cobra Pro (wireless ver). Razer built a feature rich mouse that can do it all with excellent build quality (no creaking, side flexing or M1/M2 wobble) compared to the mice from other brands. A lot of critics wanted an ultra lightweight ~50g Viper mini, not this. But for the people who care about having a feature rich mouse with excellent build quality, ability to cycle between multiple devices using different connections (Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, wired), this is a great mouse that also happens to have the latest and greatest tech for top tier gaming performance. There's a profile button on the bottom of the mouse that allows you to cycle between different profiles, which is useful if you wanted to have a profile for your laptop that turns off the RBG lighting, reduces the poll rate to 500 Hz (save battery) etc. The mouse has on-board memory, so you can save your profiles and settings, then uninstall Synapse if you so please. The only con is that the RGB settings are still not saved with the on-board memory profiles (c'mon Razer). The M1/M2 buttons have a crisp, slightly higher than normal audible click and the side buttons are placed well and feel great. The rubber side grips are molded into this model, so you cannot remove them. This is not great if they wear down, as they cannot be easily replaced like grip tape. The shape of the mouse is 99% the exact same as it's predecessor, the Viper mini. From a technical perspective, this mouse is capable of 4K Hz polling rate, but only if you purchase the HyperPolling dongle or the Dock Pro from Razer, otherwise it defaults to 1K Hz polling. The mouse is not as heavy as everyone is lamenting online, as it weighs in at ~76g. If you take off the dongle cover on the Razer Cobra Pro, you can get the mouse down to ~74g and which improves the balance in my opinion. For reference, here is how much some popular mice weigh among the big two: - Logitech G305 which is similar in size, weighs 99g. - G Pro Wireless is 80g - G Pro SuperLight is 61g - Razer Viper Ultimate is 74g - Razer Viper V2 Pro is 59g Battery life: - 170 hours on Bluetooth - 100 hours on 2.4GHz wireless (1K Hz polling) - 33 hours on 2.4 GHz wireless (4K Hz polling) Overall, I really like this mouse from Razer and personally, going up in weight from ~50g hasn't had any impact on gaming performance, I adjusted very quickly and actually don't mind the extra bit of weight (high sens). In the future, a lighter V2 with no rubber side grips would be ideal. --TLDR-- Pros: - Excellent build quality (no creaking, flexing or M1/M2 wobble) - Top tier sensor from Razer - Multi-device capable (Bluetooth to your laptop, 2.4GHz dongle in your desktop. even wired) - Gen 3 Razer optical switches (no double clicking like mechanical switches) - Mouse wheel is rubberized, feels great - Medium weight mouse at ~76g (74g if you remove the dongle cover) - USB-C connector - Top tier 2.4GHz almost zero latency wireless connection Cons: - Built-in rubber side grips (if these wear down, you're stuck with it instead of just replacing grip tape) - RGB settings aren't stored in the on-board memory, so you'll have to keep Synapse installed if you care about specific RGB settings - 4K Hz polling rate requires the additional HyperPolling dongle or Dock Pro (sold separately) - could be lighter (~60g range), but not a deal breaker Bonus review: The wired version of the Cobra is almost an exact replica of the Viper Mini wired, but with improvements to the sensor for LOD (lift off distance) and now has the Gen3 optical switches. Try this mouse and be the judge for yourself!

Its lightweight, premium build feels incredibly durable, and the customizable RGB Chroma lighting adds a personal touch to your setup. Performance-wise, the Focus Pro 30K optical sensor is a game-changer, offering 30,000 DPI sensitivity with flawless tracking. Whether I’m playing fast-paced shooters or strategy games, the mouse delivers exceptional precision and zero noticeable lag, thanks to HyperSpeed Wireless technology. The Razer Optical Mouse Switches ensure lightning-fast response times, providing a competitive edge in intense gaming scenarios. Customization is seamless with Razer Synapse software, which allows me to tweak DPI settings, program buttons, and adjust the RGB lighting with ease. The 80-hour battery life means I rarely worry about charging, and when I do, it’s quick and efficient. Overall, the Razer Cobra Pro is the ultimate wireless mouse for both casual and competitive gamers. Its combination of design, performance, and customization options makes it an exceptional value. review_title: Provides the power requirements of your USB devices while extending the available ports.
body_en: I had a problem. My monitor array at home includes a Thunderbolt hub that includes two DisplayPort and one VGA connector, and my laptop at home includes one HDMI and one additional VGA connector, but this totals only 6 screens when my laptop's primary screen is added in. My monitor array, on the other hand, includes yet another 6 screens (all but two of them are 1080p). These screens are driven by a set of mostly DisplayLink display adapters, although I have a few others that required manually installed drivers (with varying success), and some that don't advertise DisplayLink but whose drivers installed automatically anyways. Six USB-A Display adapters require a lot of power, and I ran into the limit of my workstation and Thunderbolt hub's power capacity at only 4 additional displays, and every single USB-A and USB-C port on my laptop and my dock were used up, leading to a messy snarl of wires and cables that wire ties just didn't resolve. What I like: 1. It allows me to connect my entire array of video extenders and power my entire array of monitors. It substantially cleans up the mess of cables connected to my laptop and hub by putting many of them in one place. 2. Its aluminum finish looks good on my desktop. 3. Its power supply is rated for 65w, telling me I can connect more devices before its capacity is exhausted. 4. It has a sturdy construction. What I don't like: a. Ummm, that's a tough one. Maybe it takes up additional desk space and there are a lot of cables connected to it, but hey, that's kind-of the intent. Nah, I can't say I dislike that. Caveats: - Your results may vary if you plan to use this to drive a large array of screens. My laptop has 64GB RAM and a second video card with another 6GB video RAM. I have a newer laptop at work with 128GB RAM and a second video card with 16GB video RAM that can't run my home array without overheating.

review_title: Takes up a little more space than you might think, but it definitely does what it advertises.

I have it mounted under my desk with mounting tape because it's lightweight, and it allows me to organize the cables without having to trail most of them across my desk. The unit itself has a nice, small profile, but the fact that it needs a power pack instead of just a regular cable does add to the space it takes up. Overall, it's provided me the opportunity to connect more devices and power/charge devices that were previously plugged into power adapters. So far, it's performing well, has given me more charging capacity, and I still have space left for additional devices if I decide to add more. Overall, it was worth the cost of this particular item.

review_title: Performed well until it didn't, but replaced promptly without hassle.
body_en: This USB hub worked well for 9 months then it started intermittently not communicating, then it would reconnect. All I had connected at those disconnect times were Logitech dongles for a keyboard and trackball. Difficult to diagnose, I thought the screen was freezing, perhaps a graphics card issue. Occasionally Windows issued the "USB device not connected." When the hub completely failed, the diagnosis was easy. I contacted intpw via email as suggested on their website, after a couple of efforts at diagnosis they agreed the unit was defective and replaced it promptly through Amazon. The service tech suggested that Logitech dongles should be placed as far apart at possible on the hub, they are known to interfere with each other if too close; don't know that I've ever had that problem, but took the advice. So yeah, it would have been nice if it didn't fail, but stuff happens and they replaced it. This thing is really well made, an aluminum extrusion with the board rigidly mounted inside, shielded and physically protected.

There is not much to say about this. It has a low profile and lets you expand how many USB ports you have. The first four USB A ports, starting from the left, have 5Gb/s speeds. The next two have 10Gb/s speeds. What you should know is that of the three USB C ports on the right, the first one has 10Gb/s speeds, the next two are just for power and do not handle data. If you have a phone or tablet that lets you charge it through a USB C port, you can plug it into one of those ports and it will charge. What you should know is that you need to plug this into a high-speed USB 3.2 port to get the fast speeds. It comes with a USB C to USB C data cable for plugging into your computer. Since it only gives you one USB C data port, you're not gaining any additional USB C ports since you use one from your computer and only get one in return. review_title: Solidly built powered USB hub (with a few wrinkles)
body_en: This hub has a very Apple-esque design and appears to be very solidly built. So far, it seems to perform well and as expected based on its specs. A couple of things though that are not made clear to purchasers based on the description provided: 1. The hub is provided only with a US 2-pin mains power lead. In other countries you’ll need to use a plug adaptor, else provide your own native mains cord with an IEC-C7 “figure 8” connector on the other end. At least the power brick uses that style of connector, the mains plug is not hard-wired. 2. The instructions warn you that WiFi dongles (such as those used to communicate with wireless mouse and keyboards) should not be plugged into the hub due to the risk of interference. Meaning one port on your laptop/PC will have to be used for such dongles if you have them. Not a dealbreaker, but it would have been nice to know this prior. 3. The instructions say only one HDD or two SSDs can be connected to the hub (presumably for power draw reasons). The maximum load is 900 mA (4.5 W) but it’s not clear if that is per data port (the USB standard) or in total across all data ports. This hub provides only one USB-C and two USB-A 3.1 Gen 2 data ports (10 Gbps). That’s a bit light-on these days. The remainder are USB-A 3.0 ports (5 Gbps). The two “power delivery” (non-data) USB-C ports are handy for charging devices, total power delivery max 45 W. So all up, a rating of 4 stars.

The build quality also feels solid. The housing has a nice premium feel, and it doesn’t feel flimsy despite being compact. It’s small enough to travel with if needed but works equally well as a desktop hub. One thing to keep in mind is power. Make sure your laptop charger has enough wattage to power both your laptop and any connected accessories. That’s not a fault of this hub, just something people should be aware of when setting up a dock or multi-port adapter. Pros Great selection of ports without being excessive Reliable performance Compact but well built Premium-feeling materials Works well for both travel and desktop setups Cons Requires an adequately powered USB-C charger for the best experience Port selection may not fit every specialized setup Final Thoughts This has been a great USB-C hub. review_title: I don't know how I ever lived without it.
body_en: I'm very happy with this device. My laptop doesn't have an ethernet port and only has one USB-C SuperSpeed port, so I bought an ethernet to USB-C cable to connect my ethernet switch to the Anker and into my laptop's USB-C port, and it works great. I don't need a fast internet connection for the things I do, so my service is only a 50mbps symmetrical up/down connection, and that's what I get even while transferring files from my external between other devices, charging my phone, and using composite devices. I bought the Anker 100W Compact and Foldable USB C Charger for it and it charges my S24 extremely fast. It's very well built, yet super lightweight. I love the sleek, slender design. It's the perfect size to easily slide into a pocket, store in a desk drawer, or keep handy in a laptop case or backpack. Using it is easy. Just plug it into your computer and plug your devices into it. Just make sure you have a power supply for it if you're charging or powering other devices, using external storage, or running anything else that taxes USB power. I have had ZERO connectivity issues with it — no random disconnect/reconnect blips, no failed transfers for huge amounts of data that have taken up to 45 minutes, no static his or crackle when my headset is running through it... no problems at all. It's actually kind of spooky now that I think about it... I can't recall a time I've ever had a similar device that didn't have some nuance that got under my skin, like a loose connection, random disconnections, having to reinstall the drivers all the time, or having to troubleshoot just to get it connected for the first time. The most stress I've put it through was with my keyboard connected, ethernet running through it, my S24 charging and transferring about ~20gb of pictures and videos to my 2T external HD at the same time that my laptop was transferring about ~500gb of media and documents to the HD, too, and I was surprised by how warm it DIDN'T get. My only complaint is trivial and unique to my situation — I wish output cord was longer. About six inches would do. My laptop sits up on an adjustable stand that clamps to my desk, and the end where the output cord is hangs a few inches off of my desk. This puts extra stress on the USB-C port and can wear it out faster or damage it. I haven't had a use for the HDMI port yet, but I eventually will. I use all of the other ports for my work and personal devices, though. These include: a 2tb external hard drive; a Poly Blackwire 3320 Series headset; a dongle for a wireless mouse/keyboard combo or a wired keyboard and a dongle for a wireless mouse; my Galaxy S24 charges and transfers files through it super fast; I have several thumb drives ranging from 20gb to 512gb that I regularly use; I recently bought an RCA/S Video-to-USB converter to digitize old home movies I plug into it, too.

review_title: Compact aluminum USB‑C hub with true 4K60 and fast ports
body_en: This little Yottamaster hub turned out to be a genuinely useful addition to my setup. It’s compact, lightweight, and feels sturdier than most of the plastic hubs in this price range thanks to the aluminum casing. That metal shell isn’t just for looks either — it helps keep the hub cool during long sessions, and even when I had multiple devices plugged in, it never got hot enough to worry about. The port layout is simple but well thought out. You get two USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports for fast transfers, a USB 2.0 port for a keyboard or mouse, a dedicated USB‑C PD port, and the HDMI output. The USB 3.2 ports really do hit the advertised 10Gbps speeds — moving large files to an external SSD was quick and smooth. The slower USB 2.0 port is clearly labeled “480 Mbps,” which is actually helpful so you don’t accidentally plug fast storage into the wrong spot. The HDMI port supports full 4K at 60Hz, and the picture quality is sharp and stable. It’s worth noting that your device needs to support DP Alt Mode for the video output to work, but once connected, the hub handled an external monitor without any flicker or handshake issues. I used it for both extended desktop and mirrored display, and it behaved exactly as expected. Charging performance is another strong point. The PD port supports up to 100W input, with 90W passed through to the laptop and the remaining power used to run the hub itself. Being able to charge while using all the ports at once is a big convenience, especially if you’re working with a single USB‑C port on your device. It’s also nice that the PD port is charge‑only — no confusion about whether it carries data or video. In day‑to‑day use, everything just works. No drivers, no fuss, no random disconnects. It’s small enough to toss in a laptop bag and forget about, and sturdy enough that I’m not worried about it getting banged around. For travel, office setups, or even a future mini‑PC build, it’s a clean, reliable way to expand ports without clutter. Overall, it’s a well‑made, technically solid little hub that punches above its price point.

review_title: Do you have an external drive that has a short cable?
body_en: I have a LITE-ON USB 2.0 External CD/DVD Writer Model eUAU108, manufactured in 2013, with an attached cable that is slightly less than 4 inches long. This model was an improvement over prior models, in that it requires only a single USB 2.0 connection, whereas previous models employed a Y-cable to enable connecting to 2 USB ports simultaneously for additional power. I have always felt that this drive was marginally capable of running on the 500 mA specification for USB 2.0 ports. I think this is the main reason for the ultra short cable - to minimize the voltage drop. The short cable worked OK when I was using the drive with a laptop, but attempting to use it with a computer attached to the back of my flat screen monitor is a major problem. The USB ports are about a foot above the desktop, making it necessary to support the drive in some manner. This has always been problematic. I tried using the only USB extension cable that I had, a cheap dollar store cable, and it did not work at all. My next thought was that I should purchase a higher quality, and obviously more expensive, USB cable, but I still had reservations. Would a longer cable, even of a higher quality, work? Why did LITE-ON force a short cable onto the consumer? They could have provided a USB port instead of an attached cable. I then thought of using a powered hub, which could solve the voltage/power issue, but I still wondered if there might be other signal quality issues that a longer cable might cause. I believe I was starting to overthink the matter at this point! I started looking at the market of powered hubs and discovered that there was quite a variety, from no-name cheapies to surprisingly expensive higher end units. It was easy to eliminate the no-name cheapies because there were brand names I was familiar with that were very affordable. Then I discovered that some of the hubs were rated at 10 Gbps! Gotta have that feature, right? Even though I don't have a single device faster than 5 Gbps, I justified this feature on the basis of future-proofing. I figured it would only be a matter of time before I had devices of that speed. Later on I discovered that all the USB ports on the computer attached to the back of my monitor are 10 Gbps capable – five are USB 3.2 Gen2 (10 Gbps) and one is USB4 (40 Gbps!) - additional justification for going with a 10 Gbps hub. As I looked at the 10 Gbps offerings I quickly discovered that many, if not most of them, were from RSHTECH/Rosonway. They have quite a variety of well designed, useful devices. So many options that I found it helpful to generate a table of features to more easily compare them. I finally decided to go with the RSH-H7C4 for the following reasons: • 10 Gbps on every port • both USB-A and USB-C ports • push button switch (vs. rocker type), with an indicator light, for each port • all ports support USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2), delivering a maximum of 1.5A at 5V (7.5W) per port [standard USB ports limit current to 0.5A (USB 2.0) or 0.9A (USB 3.2)] • 36W (12V/3A) DC power adapter • detachable 3.3 foot USB-C host cable (when I need to connect to a USB-A host I use a cheap adapter I purchased at a dollar store; some of the Rosonway units include a dual-headed cable with both A and C plugs!) • two year warranty It's a beautifully designed unit with a solid, weighty feel to it. Rounded edges and a thin accent band of non-anodized aluminum around each end give this hub a modern, classy appearance. With the case being narrow and slightly rounded on the bottom, one might have concern about its stability against the pushing and pulling of the connected USB cables. While it might technically be more stable with a completely flat bottom, it is surprisingly stable as is due to its weight and mass. Not at all like some of the lighter weight plastic cased devices that I have. It would take a deliberate effort to tip it over; I don't think that will be an issue. I actually do tip it over to accommodate one of my situations: the cable on my DVD drive is so short that the drive cannot lay flat when the cable is inserted into the port on the hub from above. I have to lay the hub on its side (see video). The included USB cable is heavy gauge, very thick. With my limited experience in the world of USB cables I have made two observations: 1)there is a tremendous range of cost, quality, and capabilities among the many cables on the market; 2)an extra USB cable frequently comes in handy. It would make sense to me that RSHTECH would provide a suitably high-grade cable with their hub in order to support the 10 Gbps data rate and the BC1.2 current draw capability. The fact that the USB cable is detachable is a bonus! It can be used elsewhere. I could even change it into an extension cable by the use of a gender-changing adapter. The indicator lights are a beautiful blue, quite small, but tastefull in my opinion; apparently too small for some reviewers, but I have no complaint. I would rather have them understated than overstated. The first testing I did was to connect the aforementioned LITE-ON CD/DVD writer to the computer hanging on the back of my monitor using the RSH-H7C4 hub and its included USB cable. (When the LITE-ON drive is directly attached to this computer I never have problems because the power requirement of the LITE-ON drive is easily satisfied.) I briefly tried the hub in “bus-powered” mode (without the power supply attached). I was able to read files on the DVD writer with no problem. (This was just a brief, not comprehensive, test because my main concern was testing the more power intensive task of burning a disk.) The next testing was in “self-powered” mode (with the power supply attached). I successfully burned and verified an ISO image. I then disconnected the power supply and tried to burn the image again in bus-powered mode. The burning went without any error messages, but the verification process failed. Another attempt in bus-powered mode failed during the burning process. Returning to self-powered mode (with the power supply attached), I was again able to successfully burn and verify the ISO image. It appears that when the DVD writer is attached through the hub and cable, burning a disk requires additional power beyond what the computer port is supplying (in order to power the circuitry in the hub and to compensate for loss over the length of the three foot cable). USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2) seems to do the job here. I am pleased with that! I have solved the short cable issue; I can now lay my DVD drive flat on the desk and have dependable operation. Additional testing with a much older computer, a Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 (vintage 2010), revealed an unexpected limitation: the DVD writer was unable to be recognized as a boot device by the Inspiron Mini when connected to it through the hub. As far as I can tell, this is a limitation of the older BIOS in the Inspiron. There is no way to make this system recognize an optical drive connected via a USB hub at boot up. After the system is booted the drive is able to be used with no problem. It is my understanding that the more modern BIOSes of today handle this situation in a more sophisticated manner and can detect hub-connected optical drives at bootup. I verified this by bootup tests on the computer attached to my monitor and on a modern netbook. Both of those systems were able to recognize the DVD writer at bootup with no problem when it was connected via the hub. The Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 has USB 2.0 ports that theoretically should supply enough power for the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer, but I have always felt that it was marginal. I would like to be able to supplement the power. The RSH-H7C4 is only a partial solution here. It can be used with the Inspiron for burning disks since that is a process that occurs after bootup, but in the case where I need to boot from this DVD writer I might have to first transfer the DVD image to a bootable USB thumb drive and use that instead. While not a comprehensive evaluation of the RSH-H7C4, my tests have assured me that some of my problems have been solved. I can comfortably lay the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer on the desk instead of trying to figure out how to suspend it a foot up in the air in order to attach it to the computer hanging behind my flat screen monitor. I can also use the hub for more dependable disk burning using my Inspiron Mini 1012. I am quite impressed with the RSH-H7C4 hub and RSHTECH/Rosonway. I've always been very excited by little “boxes” and devices that solve computer interconnection (and other) problems. The companies that come up with these solutions are frequently very clever. RSHTECH will now be one of the first companies I look to for such solutions. A brief look at their lineup shows devices such as: • USB switches (to share USB ports between two computers) • powered and unpowered USB hubs, some with card readers and HDMI ports • powered USB extension cables • unpowered USB extension cables with built-in signal booster chips • USB HDD/SSD enclosures • docking and cloning stations • 10 Gbps USB connected M.2 NVME/SATA SSD enclosures • 10 Gbps USB connected Magnetic M.2 NVME SSD enclosure with 100W PD RSHTECH puts an effort into including enough hard facts and specifications in their product descriptions to enable consumers to easily understand a device’s capabilities and limitations. This fact, and my favorable impression of the RSH-H7C4 hub, give me confidence to expect good performance and value with any of their products.

Review of Rosonway 7 Ports USB 3.2 Hub 36W I purchased the Rosonway 7 Ports USB 3.2 Hub 36W and tested it in two separate configurations. First with my Surface PC laptop operating Windows and second with my Mac Mini 4 operating Sequoia. The Hub, which is powered with a 36W(12V/3A) DC power adapter, comes with 7 Ports, 4 USB-C 3.2 ports and 3 USB-A 3.2 ports. It claims speeds up to 10Gbps on every port. The Hub is small and sturdy aluminum device with independent electronic switches on each port and a blue LED indicator to display power status. This enables power management over all connected devices. When I connected it to my Surface laptop PC it worked seamlessly. I was able to connect to my external mouse and keyboard, 4 thumb drives and an external backup drive. The computer recognized all the drives and could rapidly access the external backup even with all these peripherals attached and running, the hub did not get hot (only warm as would be expected). I then put the hub through an extremely tough challenge. I connected it to my Mac Mini 4 through one of the rear-facing thunderbolt/USB C ports. I then connected all my peripherals to the hub. I did not use any of the other available Mac Mini ports, only the Ronsonway Hub. I connected the following peripherals: external Kensington Trackball mouse, a Seagate Portable 4TB External Hard Drive, two thumb drives, external speakers, a Xencelabs Quick Keys, and a backup UPS device and a second hub (7-Port USB C Hub Splitter 10Gbps with 3 USB-3.2, 4 USB-3.0 Ports) – this hub was connected to a Logitech camera. All of the peripherals worked perfectly. I could open and read all the external drives (the Seagate and the 2 thumb drives) the webcam, mouse and Quick Keys all worked without problems. Even with all these peripherals including the second hub attached and running, the hub did not get hot (only warm as would be expected). I couldn’t be happier with the performance of this compact, but powerful, hub. I made a brief video if you want to see the hub and the attachments I made to the hub. One final thought, I believe this hub is a terrific economical option for expanding a laptop or desktop to accommodate an amazing array of peripherals. This hub demonstrates that a single USB C connection to a Thunderbolt 4 port on my Mac Mini, can simultaneously and seamlessly accommodate a wide array of desktop components.

review_title: Solid powered USB hub that has performed in the time I have used it.
body_en: I have been in IT long enough to know that a USB hub is one of those products that sounds simple on paper but has a surprisingly wide range of quality in practice. I have also been burned enough times by bad ones to approach any new hub with a healthy dose of skepticism. So when I say that the Rosonway powered USB hub has genuinely impressed me, I want you to understand that it is coming from someone who does not hand out compliments to peripheral hardware easily. I have had this hub for 13 days now. That might not sound like a long time, but in the context of my daily IT work, I have put it through what I would consider a serious run of testing. This is not a hub that has been sitting on a desk powering a wireless mouse dongle and a phone charger. It has been put through a ringer of a minimum of 12-14 hours 5-6 days a week. And it was used every day. With a rotating cast of demanding devices that would expose any weakness in a lesser product. Why I Came Back to Rosonway This is actually my second Rosonway hub. My first one is still running, still reliable, and was purchased specifically because I had grown so frustrated with other brands that I needed something I could actually count on. Before finding Rosonway the first time, I dealt with pretty much every problem a USB hub can throw at you — and often all at once. Devices dropping connection randomly. Transfer speeds that had no business being as slow as they were, even on a nominally high-speed hub. Units that died within weeks of purchase. Build quality that felt like it might give out at any moment. When you work in IT, unreliable hardware is not just an annoyance — it is a productivity problem and, at times, a professional one. The last thing I need in the middle of a task is a hub that decides to drop a device or throttle my speeds without warning. After going through several different brands and experiencing those issues repeatedly, I finally landed on Rosonway. My first unit solved all of those problems and has kept solving them ever since. So when I needed more ports, the decision to go back to Rosonway was not really a decision at all. It was the obvious move based on earned trust. Sure you could go with more notorious brands, but the bang for my buck on this brand has been optimal. Daily Use in an IT Context My use case is not casual. I run this hub daily as part of an IT work setup that includes both a PC and a Mac, and I switch between the two regularly. Cross-platform reliability is something I specifically look for and specifically test, because a hub that works beautifully on Windows but causes headaches on macOS is only solving half my problem. This one works correctly on both. No configuration differences, no quirks on one platform that do not exist on the other. It simply works the same way on both machines, which is exactly what you want. The range of peripherals I have connected through this hub over the past 13 days is wide. I have been running a wired USB-C to 3.5mm DAC for my Corsair headset with microphone — and I want to flag this one specifically, because audio devices are often where cheaper hubs start to show their weaknesses. A DAC demands consistent, clean power delivery. Any instability shows up immediately as audio dropout, static, or microphone signal issues. This hub has delivered clean, uninterrupted audio and microphone performance every single time. Beyond that, I have put external hard drives, thumb drives, and an SSD dock through this hub. External drives and SSD docks are about the most demanding things you can connect to a USB hub from a power and bandwidth standpoint. Drives pulling sustained power while transferring data will expose any inadequacy in a hub's power management quickly. I have had no issues — transfers run at expected speeds, the SSD dock behaves as if it is connected directly to the machine, and nothing has dropped or stuttered. I have connected all of these devices in various combinations, not just one at a time. Running multiple demanding peripherals simultaneously is where a lot of hubs start to fall apart, and this one has handled every configuration I have thrown at it without complaint. No Drivers, No Nonsense One of the things I appreciated immediately was the plug-and-play experience. There were no extra drivers to hunt down and install. On both the PC and the Mac, I connected the hub and everything worked. That is the experience it should always be, but it is not always the experience you get — especially when you are working across two different operating systems. Anyone who has spent time troubleshooting driver issues for what should be a simple USB hub knows how much time that can waste. The fact that this product required none of that was noticed and appreciated from day one. The Physical Setup The cable length on this hub is one of the practical details that does not always get mentioned in reviews but genuinely matters in a real workspace. It is long enough to allow for flexible positioning without being so long that it becomes a cable management problem. I was able to position the hub where it actually needed to be on my desk rather than compromising based on where the cable could reach. Small thing, but it adds up. The hub is powered, which is worth emphasizing for anyone who has tried to run demanding devices off a bus-powered hub and wondered why things were not working right. Having dedicated power through the included adapter means each port has what it needs to perform, even with multiple devices pulling from it simultaneously. For the kind of peripherals I am running — drives, an SSD dock, a DAC — powered is not optional. It is required. This hub delivers that without any hesitation. Thirteen Days and Counting I want to be honest about what 13 days of heavy daily use tells you and what it does not. It does not give you years of long-term reliability data. What it does give you is a solid read on whether a product is going to perform under real working conditions without hand-holding. I have not been gentle with this hub, in terms of use. I have been plugging and unplugging devices frequently, running demanding transfers, switching between operating systems, and connecting combinations of peripherals that test the power distribution. In all of that, I have not encountered a single failure, dropout, connection issue, or performance problem. That tracks with my experience with my first Rosonway hub, which is still running well after a year and half. The consistency between the two units tells me something about how Rosonway approaches quality control. It is one thing for one product to perform well. It is another for two separate purchases, at different times, to both deliver the same reliable experience. Who This Hub Is For If you are running a setup with demanding peripherals — external drives, audio devices, docking solutions — and you need something that will perform reliably across PC and Mac without driver headaches or connection instability, this hub is worth serious consideration. If you have been through the frustrating cycle of buying cheaper hubs, dealing with the problems they inevitably bring, and then replacing them, I understand that cycle because I lived it for longer than I should have. The Rosonway powered USB hub is not the flashiest product in the world. It does not need to be. It has been dependable so far. It does exactly what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring you to babysit it or troubleshoot it or work around its limitations. In the world of peripheral hardware, that kind of consistency is a huge bonus in my line of work. Two for two on Rosonway products. I will be back if I need more ports. I am satisfied with my purchase.

TLDR: This is a fast, powerful, versatile 7-port USB 3.2 Gbps hub that gives you lots of ports which is especially useful for modern laptops which often only have one port. This connects to a laptop/PC via a USB-C cable. It also needs a power cable to function so make sure you are close to a wall outlet or even better, a surge protector. You get 7 ports - 4 USB-C ports and 3 classic USB-A ports. They are all version 3.2 ports with a speeds up to 10Gbps. You can toggle each one on/off with the buttons on the side. The ports have a light that comes on with enabled. It's got sturdy aluminum body so it's safe to transport and won't get damaged in your backpack. Performance‑wise, it’s handled everything I’ve thrown at it. I’ve had multiple drives, a mouse, a keyboard, and a couple of random accessories plugged in at the same time, and it didn’t choke or overheat — just got slightly warm, which is normal. The 10Gbps ports definitely move files quickly, and the external power supply keeps everything stable. It’s not meant to fast‑charge big devices, but for data and powering smaller gear, it’s been rock‑steady. If you need a dependable, powered hub with a mix of USB‑A and USB‑C ports and don’t want to spend a fortune, this one’s easy to recommend. The company: I'm a big fan of this brand. I own other products from them, and they are all great quality.

review_title: Quality & design issues surfaced during usage
body_en: August 2023 update: On the 3rd week, my 2nd unit started to blink two hard drive connections on and off with only 3 ports switched on. Therefore rating is reduced to 1 star from 2. Initially, my 2nd unit successfully wrote 350 Gb drive to drive across this hub without any buffering errors (buffering errors are what usually goes wrong in such tests). Speed was about 40 - 70 mb per second for nominally-sized files. However was unable to complete a chkdsk on a mounted drive without terminating in a unidentifiable error (again usually what happens with bad hubs). My first unit which was returned had a bad port #3 (counting from the end plugs) and was causing disk errors evident in the Windows event viewer, which actually were errors when chkdsk was used (you cannot always trust the event viewer drive errors as Windows presumes any drive is where you left it from your last Windows session, so if you move it, or it is new to the location on its USD bus, the event viewer will scream bloody murder until it learns the new location, where it will then proclaim the drive is healthy). There appears to be a design deficiency in the hub: on both units I tested, there was too much noise on the final port #10 to plug in a cam. The cam image was very noisy and unusable. Plugging in the cam at the first port works around this design problem. Apparently, there is inadequate noise containment within the hub body, and this can cause slower transfer rates for hard drives and bad images for cams. Given the wide variety of hubs and potential for hub problems, and quality variance of Asian-pacific manufacturers, I am going to keep this one. Be sure to check each port when you receive yours.

review_title: VIA Labs chipset - so far so good
body_en: So far so good. Will update review if anything changes - have audio interface and few devices plugged in, external hard drive, sd card reader - no issues. For anyone curious about the chipset used, it's VIA Labs: VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_0822 (USB 3.2 hub) Primary 3-port hub + 1 downstream port (USBC) VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_0822 (USB 3.2 hub) Secondary 4-port hub off that downstream port (USBA) VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_2822 (USB 2.1 companion hubs) This was the only information I couldn't find before purchase, and was exactly what I was looking for - previously purchased a Amazon Basics 7 port usb3.1 hub and kept on getting errors in device manager. review_title: A hub is not a dock. This is a very good USB-C hub
body_en: Does what a hub ought to do - which is to say, you can plug it into one USB-C port and it will make power and data connectivity available to four downstream USB-C devices. The big caveats are that the host cable is extremely short and the power made available to downstream devices is significantly reduced from what the host provides. It's still a five star device because these short cables are universally present on all USB-C hubs, and the power limitations are less severe than other similar products that I have tested. Most importantly, the data connectivity offered by this unit is excellent, and it's extremely portable, being barely larger than the connectors it contains. I would still very much prefer a version of this device with a USB-C female connector on the back instead of the permanently attached short cable but apparently there are valid technical reasons that USB-C hubs are not made in this way. Devices that offer more power and better cabling options are now classified as docks rather than hubs, they tend to be based on Thunderbolt rather than plain old USB-C, and some of these docks are quite excellent, but they are comparatively very expensive. This particular device is just a hub, it is very affordable compared to a dock, and it's as good as USB-C hubs get.

It's super handy for connecting all my gear, from cameras to a keyboard, and I've had zero issues with performance. The pass-through charging up to 100W is also a lifesaver, keeping my laptop juiced up while I use the hub. Plus, the compact design and durable build mean I can toss it in my bag without a second thought. Belkin truly understands what users need in a reliable multi-port adapter.

I also like that it works with a variety of devices, including laptops, tablets, and desktops that support USB C. The build quality feels solid, and everything connects securely without feeling loose. If you also need USB A, HDMI, or SD card slots, you will likely need an additional adapter. Depending on your setup, that may limit its versatility. Overall, this is a dependable and portable USB C hub that delivers fast performance and convenient charging. If your devices primarily use USB C, it is an excellent solution for expanding connectivity while keeping your workspace simple and organized.

Pros: Compact design and layout. The first port even has pass through current up to 100W to charge smaller devices. Easy to open packaging. Good "click" locking mechanism for the connections. No speed reduction when using multiple drives/storage devices. Con (More of an Improvement): I wished the upstream power cord was removable, which would make it easy to store and could use different lengths if needed. The current 12-inch one is not bad, but can cause issue to fold while carrying or storing. Bottomline: For $35 you can't go bad with a good brand that has been around. I will give it a 4.6/5.0.

And I'm sure it does all those things beautifully, but what it doesn't do is support charging of my iPhone..... which is a bit of a deal-breaker, really. Looking back, I see that the description doesn't actually mention support for iPhone 15 Pro, but iPad Pro and Mac compatibility (and support for supposedly universal USB-C devices) clearly doesn't include the iPhone. Very happy to accept that the reason for that is Apple and their outright stupid insistence on control of everything, but it doesn't really help me..... I've often bought Belkin accessories and peripherals and it's a brand I trust, so my "Value for money" and "Charging power" scores relate only to my immediate experience and inability to charge my iPhone. UPDATE 3 APR 2024: I've left all my ignorant waffle above in place in case any other users find the difficulty I had - and judging by the numbers who can't get their iPad to charge, there are several of us. I did uprate my "star" rating as the problem isn't Belkin and not even Apple, for a change :-) After some digging I found reference to a recommended power supply delivery of 100W, so phoned Belkin UK Support - and got straight through! Very helpful bloke took the details, looked up the specs, and confirmed that the MINIMUM permissible power supply to the hub is 85W and the RECOMMENDED rating is 100W. Less than that, and the hub won't allow pass-through to protect other components against possible excess current. Unfortunate, but I guess I'll have to shell out for an adequate PSU. My high opinion of Belkin kit is even higher now having experienced their support function. Very good indeed.

review_title: Hub de 6 puertos USB de alta velocidad
body_en: ✷ If you have a computer or laptop that lacks high-speed USB ports, this device is the quality and reliable extension that you may have been looking for for a long time. I think it's perfect, but let's see. ✷ This adapter device was born from the need that there are numerous laptops with a very compact profile, which lack USB ports in which to connect more peripherals or specific accessories. It is not difficult to find that in many of them, especially in 13" notebooks, there are only a couple of USB-A ports available, and at most one USB-C. This hub not only expands the number of ports, but also combines 3 USB-C 3.2 Gen2 type ports, and 3 USB-A 3.0. ► Presented in a small white box, we find this compact adapter made entirely of aluminum. The appearance is in titanium color. metallic, makes it especially sober and elegant. Its measurements are quite compact: 12 cm x 4.5 cm x 1.5 cm and only 90 gr. The connection cable is not braided nylon but it looks correct. However, the encapsulation of the USB-C male socket is made of premium aluminum. webcam, gamepad, our Smartphone or even a 2.5” hard drive. It is in storage devices where this extra speed will be most noticeable, especially if they can be connected to type 3.2 ports, since at a data transfer speed of 10Gbps, there will not be the same bottleneck as can happen in USB 3.0 type ports. which go at 5 Gbps. ► It also has a USB-C 3.0 PD (Power Delivery) input port: Passthrough charging port of up to 100 W (actual 80W, since the Hub itself consumes 20W). Keep in mind that this port can only charge your laptop through the USB-C port if it supports PD (like that of the Macbook Pro, for example). In addition, it is recommended to use a minimum 65 W charger so that this adapter is capable of all its tasks. This port does not supply charge to what is connected to it, it only receives power from the charger to make the passthrough or bridge to your computer and charge it through the other USB-C male cable that is fixed to the cable. Also keep in mind that this USB-C port on the hub DOES NOT allow you to transfer data, that is what the other 3.1 port that is right next to it is for. ► It also has a 4K HDMI output. In it, you can connect your computer to your TV, Projector or monitor through this port. It supports 4K at 30 Hz, so you will not have quality problems. You just have to connect it via an HDMI cable with 4K support to enjoy a resolution of 3840x2160. 💢 During use and tests carried out, the behavior has been as expected, giving much higher reading and writing rates than with my previous USB 3.0 Hub. It should be taken into account that the maximum nominal theoretical speed of 10 Gbit/s of USB-C 3.2 is difficult to achieve because there are many other factors that can influence performance (from the computer hardware itself, to the operating system itself, the load of tasks at that moment, or if the internal hard drive is in use, or if we even have an Antivirus installed and its configuration). Even after connecting 3 simultaneous peripherals and working for a couple of hours, the Hub has barely warmed up. Furthermore, since its entire surface is made of aluminum, if it gets hot, it will quickly dissipate the accumulated heat. 📌 As the only “downside”, I would have liked a typical velvet bag to have been included, to prevent it from being scratched (or scratched) when I put it in the briefcase next to the laptop. But hey, for what it costs you can't ask for much more. ✪ CONCLUSION: ⭐ Very good expansion hub but at a price that can be a little scary, since the €70 that is asked for it is not enough to buy it impulsively. I have to say that the quality is outstanding, and that its moderate size and lightness make it a good ally for your Notebook. Totally recommended, if you were looking for something similar. 💬 I hope that this review and what I have commented has been useful to you. 👀
