review_title: Poor room light or High Fstop performance
body_en: My biggest problem with this camera is that in normal room light performance (without flash) is sub par, even worse than my Fuji A700 compact. The camera fails to freeze even the slightest motion without flash under normal room light. IT behaves better with 1/80s shutter spped at iso 1600 at normal room light (6, 65W floodlight bulbs in a 11x20 room). But at iso 1600 and shutter speed 1/80, the picture quality is not acceptable, pretty dark and grainy. Surprsingly my compact Fuji A700 does a better job in the same light (it also beat canon sd1000 compact) in the same test. I was hoping that I would get good normal light performance from a DSLR (espacially D60 with its good reviews) but I was wrong. Pros: Good auto focussing, 3 points is more than enough for a normal user. Single point is even more predictable. Good shoe to shot time and flash recycle time. Update: After 3 more months of use and reading the manual 3 more times I have concluded this is just a 2 star camera & not worth the money at all. The problem continues to be its low light sensitivity (or the lack of it). It keeps manifesting itself in different ways. Lately I have been having problems with its low light sensitivity when I use high Fstop numbers like F10-F16 indoors with flash. At those values I am forced to use ISO800 so that the picture will not be dark and even then the picture is not great. I am now convinced that Ken Rockwell was right in his review about the low light issue with the sensor in this camera... Only if I had read his review before buying mine.. Instead I went by then 4.5 star rating on this site & ended up wasting my money... In my view this camera is good only for brigthly lit outdoor conditions or just indoor potraits with flash. In those conditions a good point & shoot can do as good a job!!! If you want to use the D60 indoors with flash for groups pictures where some subjects are 4 feet behind the focus point, you will be utterly dissapointed because that require F10-F16 to preserve details of people in the background & this camera sucks indoors at F10-F16 even with flash & good living room light. Now Ken rockwell seems to think D40 is much better under such low light conditions, if Nikon would wanted to make me happy I would be more than willing to exchange this with a D40... As it is is near useless to me right now.... Save your money & stay away from the D60....

If you are used to a compact point-and-shoot and want to overcome the shortcomings of these cameras, then consider the Nikon D60. This camera is designed for newcomers to DSLRs and Nikon wants you to feel at home with this camera. The size and weight is just slightly more than a deluxe point-and-shoot with lots more options for those who want to take photography more seriously. Among the major reasons for buying this camera is its sharp pictures due to Nikon's lens technology which now includes a vibration reduction lens to keep your photos steady. The sensor cleaner is a big plus to keep those images clear. You have the option of using the camera on automatic or trying out many of Nikon's built-in options for editing your shots. There are very few negatives. If you are used to the pricing with a point-and-shoot, a DSLR camera looks like sticker shock. But when you realize all the benefits you are getting, it makes sense. Only other negative is that with more and more cameras raising the bar with mega-pixels, one wonders why Nikon couldn't have gone to a 12MP resolution in the D60. But for most of us, 10MP should be fine. All-in-all this is one great camera value. You get the lightweight small configuration of a point-and-shoot in a DSLR with all the benefits that the D60 offers.

review_title: Uno zaino che sa il fatto suo!

review_title: Small, light, but can carry a lot of gear ... great value in my opinion
body_en: Bought it for a trip to England and used it every day for 3 weeks. review_title: My third Espro, the first glass P3. It's that good
body_en: I bought my first Espro (a 32 oz. double-walled stainless steel model) in 2015 - mainly for its insulation as I like to keep my coffee hot while consuming 3 cups each morning. It proved to be a better alternative to the several classic glass French presses my wife and I have used over the years – for several reasons that equally apply to the P3 (which I first learned about reading NY Times Wirecutter). What’s to Like about the P3 (pics included) • Very effective double micro-filter with silicon seals. Some reviewers find this filter tedious to clean and overkill on filtration (I’ll address both issues) but I’m a big fan. The filtration system is as good as it gets in keeping grounds out of one’s coffee cup, and trapping residues that can appear in roasted coffee. Using the plunger takes more effort as the finer the grounds the more they will cling to the walls of the filter, impeding the flow and requiring more pressure to squeeze the plunger. But the good news: it is those same fine grounds that escape conventional French press filters, and that end up spoiling a cup of coffee. They just don’t get through. Plus, the filtration method minimizes the “extraction” process (it continues as the grounds sit in hot water) that can make the last cup bitter. • Dishwasher safe: The micro-filter is easy to disassemble, clean and re-assemble (see two pics). It may seem like a chore initially, but the filters are quite easy to take apart using a simple counterclockwise twist of the outermost filter from the plunger. A ½ inch twist is all that’s needed. Though Espro recommends hand-washing the entire unit, we put the plunger and disassembled filter in the dishwasher. It has survived over 100 washings so far without a glitch. Re-assembly is just as easy (see pics). Just align the slot on the outer filter with the tab on the inner filter and give it a clockwise twist to snap it back into place. • Easy to remove the glass carafe from its plastic housing for cleaning. Espro has incorporated a clever design for this. There’s a plastic tab (flange) affixed to the glass carafe (see pic) which, when it’s in the correct “pouring” position sits below the top ring of the plastic housing with handle, keeping the glass body securely in place. Just grip the top of the glass carafe, turn it until the tab sits directly above the handle and lift (see pics). Just reverse the steps to put the glass carafe securely back in the plastic housing. That said, rather than disassembling the glass body after each use we put the entire press in the dishwasher. No problems experienced. • Two water levels. There’s both a “max” and “min” setting on the glass carafe so that you can choose how much coffee to brew (see pic). The difference is about 1 cup of coffee. What you may not to Like • Coffee does not stay as hot as it does with Espro’s insulated brushed steel models. • Wasted coffee tradeoff (?): It’s debatable. This is an issue for some reviewers, but not for me. Unlike conventional French presses the Espro filtration method ends up with about 5 ounces of coffee and sludge remaining in the carafe after plunging it, which sits just above the plastic housing (see pic). You’ll get less wastage with a conventional press, but you’ll also get more grounds and bitterness towards the last cup. My take: I’m happy to trade off those 5 ounces to enjoy 27 ounces of very good coffee.

review_title: A better than average French press
body_en: My espresso machine died after a decade and I decided to try a French press again. I ordered the P3, whole beans and a Haribo ceramic burr hand grinder. The overall improvement in coffee flavor and enjoyment have been remarkable. It took a few days to find the right beans, grind fineness, amount of coffee and brew time to satisfy my taste, but it was worth the effort. Now, I consistently use 25 grams of a single source Ethiopian dark roast, a finer than recommended grind (I like a strong flavor), fill my 32 oz P3 to the “min” mark and brew for 4 minutes. I actually get up earlier in the morning, eager to have my first cup. Of course, it’s mostly the coffee and brew recipe that determines the taste, but the press plays a roll too. I’ve had Bodums and other brands and they all allowed sludge to get through and end up at the bottom of my cup. Eventually the rather coarse metal screens will deform at the edges and allow larger grounds to pass to the top side. That doesn’t happen with the P3. There are two silicone wipers that seal tightly to the glass and force all the liquid to go through the screens. The first screen filters out all but the smallest coffee particles while the second screen blocks those. It’s nice to have sludge-free coffee. To those reviewers who say their coffee was too weak, you have complete control of strength. Add more coffee, or use a finer grind, or brew longer, or use a darker roast. Use a kitchen scale rather than a spoon to measure if you want day-to-day consistency. A spoonful of a finer grind weighs more than a coarser grind. Weight is more accurate than volume for predicting strength. For those who say the plunger requires a lot of force to depress, use a coarser grind. If there are lots of fine particles, those will clog the screen and slow down the plunger. Maybe get a burr grinder. Burrs produce more consistent particle sizes. The spinny metal bladed spice grinders create every size particle from large chunks to fine powder. Those fine ones will clog the filter baskets for sure. Most grocery store grinders are burr machines and do a better job than the spice grinders. I recommend being patient and pushing the plunger down very slowly, like over 30 seconds. Pushing quickly causes churn which stirs up the grounds and causes even more clogging. Pushing really hard can force grounds to bypass the filters and push past the seals. For those who say it’s hard to clean, I find it is as easy/hard as any other French press. I pour the grounds through a fine mesh sieve and tap it into my compost pail. A once over with a soapy sponge removes the coffee oils from the glass. The screens usually just need a rinse. Although I prefer to hand wash, the instructions say that all parts can go on the top rack of the dishwasher. If this is too much trouble, you might want a Keurig. For those who say it wastes a lot of coffee, I’ve measured what remains after you’ve poured your last cup. On my 32 ounce P3, once the grounds were removed, there were 5 fluid ounces of very sludgy liquid trapped below the screens. I wouldn’t want to drink it so I don’t think of it as waste. But if this is important to you, you might consider a pour-over brewer instead where nearly every drop ends up in your cup. For those that say it’s cheaply made, it is their least expensive entry-level model. I find it robust enough to use every day. If you want something sturdier, they have other models with borosilicate glass (this model has plain glass) and metal frames. I chose the Espro French press based on a recommendation from the New York Times product reviewing site Wirecutter. I chose a French press over other types of brewers based on the YouTube videos of coffee expert James Hoffmann. I recommend both sources.

review_title: The double filters on this mean you don't need as good a grinder
body_en: I bought this along with a super high-quality grinder, and discovered that I kinda only needed one or the other. The mesh filters are fine enough on this that you can get away with a relatively crappy grinder. You can even use regular pre-ground coffee, and it'll come out okay. With a normal glass/single layer mesh press, using regular grounds will result in actual sludge in the bottom of your cup. With this unit, the Costco bulk ground coffee will leave some fines in your cup, but will work fine otherwise; the second layer of screening is good enough to keep the sludge at bay. If, on the other hand, you have a high quality, consistent grinder, you can buy a less expensive press and do fine. That said, pairing this with a good grinder makes absolutely *splendid* coffee. You don't necessarily need both, but I doubt you'll regret the purchase. The double filters can also help you calibrate your grinder; if the inner filter is getting many grounds on it, you probably want a slightly coarser grind. This unit is tall and skinny, and does better with a tall sink for cleaning. If you're trying to rinse it out upstairs in a standard bathroom sink, you should be able to do it, but it'll take a little maneuvering. The actual cleaning process is very easy, although you do have to clean two little baskets instead of one. It takes a wee bit longer than cleaning a standard press. The build quality seems good. Oh, one other note: because of the filter design, you end up with some coffee left in the bottom that you can't drink. You're using a more water than normal, so it takes more grounds than you're probably expecting. Further, French presses need more grounds for the same amount of coffee, because they're ground coarse and use a shorter brewing time. (normally 4 minutes.) I use six tablespoons of coffee per batch, and I get two 16-ounce cups out of it. With my older drip brewer, it took only four tablespoons. In exchange, the quality is *vastly* better, you can use almost any grounds, and after you've plunged it, the coffee stays excellent for at least an hour. Seems well worth it to me, but if your coffee budget is small, the higher consumption might be something to consider.

review_title: White Espro7 18oz: a great upgrade with some trade offs
body_en: TLDR: hotter longer, much less grit, harder to clean, high minimum brew requirements, poor powder coat finish, great customer service. I bought this as an upgrade to my body glass French press. Overall it is a much better press. It’s hotter longer and the dual filters do a fantastic job. Before, at the end of my coffee, it was almost unbearable. It was like gritty sludge. It was like drinking dirt. Now with the espro 7, it’s much less, and what does get through is so fine, that I can drink the last drop. It’s hotter longer, but it’s not vacuum insulated. It stays hot for 1 hour, warm after another 30 minutes. After that its Luke warm. It’s harder to clean but not by much. With glass, I can just rinse and dump it out, set it to dry and it’s good to go. By comparison, the espro filters clean very easily. In fact, the long term maintenance is probably easier. But the stainless steel press doesn’t rinse as easily. It might still have some residue and require a brush on daily use. My biggest gripe about this is the high minimum requirements. I usually just brew enough to make one cup, but this requires 2 tablespoons of grounds and enough for 1 and a half cups of coffee. The way the filter is, it seems like more water gets trapped in the bottom, and that’s why it needs more water. It’s not a big deal, but I grind my beans each use, so it doubles my grinding time and consumes my beans faster. These are bigger and heavier than a glass press. My powder coat was chipped under the handle and even had some rust built up on it. I contacted the company directly and they’re sending me a new one free of charge. And I get to keep the old one! (which still works just fine) Also the lid is painted white, but it’s plastic and not a sturdy powder coat. It scuffs easily after just a couple days of use. I believe the stainless steel (no powder coat) option has a stainless steel lid. The video attached shows what very little grit does make it into the cup. I have a $2800k fancy espresso/latte/cappuccino maker that grinds fresh beans and I use the plain old coffee pot way more because I drink too much coffee to make cup after cup, I want the whole carafe. It is an excellent coffee maker for the price, the flavor is very intense (personal taste is a very good thing), it is very easy to use and the automatic ignition is very easy to use. The appearance is very modern, I would buy another one without thinking!

review_title: Looks Great, Works Great, Tastes Great
body_en: I got this coffee maker a little over 2 years ago, mainly because of its aesthetics, specifically the design and layout were visually pleasing to me compared to other coffee makers. Also all my appliances are black and stainless. On the two cup setting, it takes about 6 minutes to brew. When it's done the coffee is really hot, and I have to wait about 5 minutes before drinking it, or drop in an ice cube and I can start drinking in about 30 seconds to a minute. I found a combination of things with this coffee maker that turns a good cup of coffee into a great one. The ninja branded measuring spoon that comes with it is more important than you might think. They've literally hit the nail on the head regarding the exact amount of coffee grounds that should be used. It's very simple, one flat scoop for every standard size cup of coffee you want, and remember the word flat. Also there's markers on the water tank so scoops and water match up. I personally found if I use a flat scoop of coffee grounds, not letting the coffee grounds be higher than that, it tastes perfect every time for me. So I would say that's a huge key to a great cup of coffee on this device. Next up, paper filters improved the taste significantly! The goldish mesh metal filter that comes in the box does not filter out all the coffee grounds. I even tried other brands of metal filters to see if they improved that, but it didn't. You will likely have some coffee grounds in the bottom of your coffee cup if you stick with the included metal reusable filter. At first I didn't think it was very many coffee grounds, but then one day I immediately poured the coffee into a glass after brewing it. Then I held the glass above my head and shined a flashlight at the bottom, and there were a lot more grounds that I saw that way, than when I was getting close to finishing a cup of coffee. Meaning, I was likely swallowing a lot of grounds and would have never known that. So I stopped using the Ninja metal filter and started buying and trying #4 cone paper filters and that did 4 things. 1. No more coffee grounds in my coffee cup. 2. No more upset stomach after drinking coffee. 3. The oily stuff that kind of floated to the top of the coffee was gone. 4. The taste of the coffee significantly improved. I would strongly suggest trying a box of paper filters to see if it improves the taste for you. Do not attempt to use a paper filter and the mesh filter at the same time. I tried that once and it significantly reduces the flow of the coffee out of the filter area. This causes the water to build up in that filter area and overflow from there on to your countertop. In closing, this is a good coffee maker, but if you use flat scoops, a good brand of paper filters, and purified water, I think those might be the keys to turning a good cup of coffee into a great one.

review_title: Clear, detachable reservoir separates this coffee maker from the masses.
body_en: I've owned this coffee maker over a month now and love it. Intuitive-to-operate controls and a very attractive appearance are among its virtues. Of course, hot water dripping over coffee grinds isn't rocket science and is something most coffee makers do comparably well, and the Ninja likewise makes excellent-tasting coffee. Other reviews were mildly critical of the "sneak a cup" functionality, but I've found it on par with that of my last two coffee makers (Krups and Cuisinart). Yes, a couple of drops of coffee will still splash on the hot plate while you pull the carafe out, but I've never used or seen a pot yet that didn't do that, and the spring mechanism on this carafe is at least as robust as any I've seen on other coffee makers. Where this pot really shines is in the clear, detachable water reservoir. That obviously offers you the (completely?) unique option of detaching the tank to fill it over the sink before brewing, which I've done a few times and anticipated doing regularly. Frankly, however, I find it unnecessary because the reservoir itself provides an unusually large opening/target for pouring directly from my filtered water pitcher. But there are other benefits to the reservoir design, including the fact that it allows you to easily monitor the conditions inside . . . i.e., when the moist environment inevitably leads to mildew, you will know it (and, because the reservoir is transparent to any ambient sunlight, mold/mildew should theoretically take longer to manifest in many kitchens.) More importantly, you'll be able to easily clean the reservoir in a sink of hot soapy water (with a little bleach) without repeated electric cleaning and rinse cycles for the whole brewer, followed by awkward attempts to wipe the nooks and crannies of the integral, typically black reservoir with a white paper towel to see if any undesirable residues remain. But perhaps the greatest advantage of this design is in what it will save you if you should *ahem* forget to put your carafe in place before you hit "brew." I've only done this twice in my life but, ironically, both times occurred within the last six weeks: once with my last Krups pot and once with this new Ninja. (Put aside for the moment what such forgetfulness might be saying about me.:-) At the very least, I gained valuable, first-hand experience in how the Ninja's design saved my a$$ while the typical integral design on the Krups resulted in a ruined coffee maker, which prompted my purchase of the Ninja in the first place.) When you fail to put the carafe under the filter spout on a coffee maker that offers the increasingly ubiquitous "sneak a cup" feature, the spring mechanism on the filter holder is never engaged and the water that's dripping down over your grinds to make coffee is never given proper egress below. So your mistake may go unnoticed for quite some time since you won't hear the kind of gushing and sizzling sound that an older model without the sneak a cup feature would produce when dripping coffee is merrily dispensing and burning on the naked hotplate below. Instead, the water stays in the filter holder, eventually having nowhere to go but over the sides, which, on the vast majority of drip coffee makers, means that the brewed coffee--complete with floating grinds--will spill over and back into the reservoir itself. That is exactly what happened to my Krups, and, despite hours of repeated cleaning cycles and an aborted effort to dismantle the innards, I realized the pot was shot (no pun intended) and would never process water properly through its (clogged) pump pathway again. Enter the Ninja. After making delicious coffee for a week or so, I, once again, got distracted by something (probably my Yorkie yapping to get out for a morning pee) and neglected to actually seat the carafe on the coffee maker before hitting brew. When I got back in, I noticed the problem just before the brewing coffee was about to overflow the filter holder. The difference was, even had I been a bit later, I would have only had to deal with a messy countertop and not a ruined $80+ coffee maker. In other words, if the Ninja coffee filter overflows, the brewed coffee will NOT go back into the reservoir because the latter is physically higher and isolated from the former in a way that would not permit that. So, should you repeat my negligence, you will hear coffee suddenly dripping on your hotplate and counter top, but you won't have to buy a new coffee maker. The only "negative" to the pot is that the carafe lid does not flip up via the common thumb depression above the handle. You have to slide/turn it to remove, which is more easily done with two hands. But this is a very, very minor ding in my view and not worth deducting a star for an otherwise very well-designed, highly practical, and elegant-looking appliance.

review_title: Great coffee maker with all the features I need
body_en: I've been using this coffee maker every day for over a month, and I have zero complaints. The coffee comes out consistently great, and since I usually brew 4 cups, the Small Batch setting has been perfect. I use disposable paper filters instead of the included reusable one because it's more convenient for me to just throw them away after brewing. Cleanup is quick and easy. I've also tested the Keep Warm and Delay Brew features, and both work exactly as expected. The coffee stays at a good temperature without tasting burnt, and the scheduled brewing has been reliable every time. Overall, it's been a fantastic coffee maker with no issues, and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a dependable machine that consistently makes great-tasting coffee.

review_title: Actually does improve the flavor of coffee compared to others. Capable, but not super well designed
body_en: UPDATE: For our second brew, I ran it on "Classic" instead of "Rich". I really was a significantly superior brew. It tasted good with the old machine, but really fine with this one. Now after over a week of use- it's a consistent result every day, and a cup of coffee is, indeed, superior with this machine and all else being equal. I found another issue, though. There's a gap between the back of the carafe lid and the handle. Steam escapes there, and it gets very hot. I have fairly large hands and I tend to put my thumb there. I have gotten burned a couple of times. It's painful but not long lasting. It's not the steam alone, but the fact that the little bit of steam heats the material for the entire brew time plus serving time. Cleaning is getting burdensome. The carafe needs a re-design. I got this to replace (?) a very basic Mr. Coffee that is about 5 years old, that is one of my favorite examples of design. It's as simple as can be: an on/off switch and a carafe that is capacious and very easy and fast to clean. It has very few right angle areas that would make it hard to clean. (They have changed the design since we bought it, and not for the better.) It still works. This Ninja is nice, and the filter basket will barely sit on the scale while I weigh the grounds into it, but it's going to tip over, and often. Once the coffee is made, you can't pour all of it from the carafe, because the plastic rim extends around the edge and into the lip, and it has a square edge. The lid of the carafe, has a strange pipe that extends to near the bottom of the pot. Why? You'd have to use a round brush to clean it well. I've made one pot of coffee so far. I used the rich setting. My wife liked it, but I thought it was much more bitter than yesterday's coffee. It was visibly darker (remember, I weigh the grounds, so that's constant). I found the liquid measure to be the same as the coffee make we've been using. Tomorrow I will try the "classic" setting. I don't really need another clock to set, or a timer, or really any of the features this sports beyond "on/off". I will also mention that the reservoir works well. But it's clear plastic. So with our regular water, it will get mineral spots (and it's virtually impossible to clean with all the strange grooves and right angles). So we have to use distilled water. I like a spotless kitchen. (The reservoir in the old one doesn't need hand cleaning because it's mostly black plastic with a frosted window to gauge water level. It much much easier to see the water level with this Ninja, though.)

I've had the 12 cup model for about 1.5 years now and have been happy with it. It brews good coffee, is easy to use and easy to clean. My only complaints are the buttons are somewhat "stiff" to press compared to my old Cuisinart and the printing is rather small for older eyes but not an issue on a daily basis. I broke the carafe about a year ago and it was pricey to replace but at least it was available. My favorite feature is the removable reservoir which makes it simple to keep clean. I like to get it ready to brew the night before and my old Cuisinart would get microbial gunk growing in the reservoir which was extremely difficult clean out and probably not healthy. No such issue with the Ninja. I just leave the lid off the reservoir after brewing and it drys out very quickly. Plus it is easy to clean out if needed.

I LOVE the Ninja drip coffee maker! 1. The coffee tastes fresh. 2. The heat plate keeps the coffee in the pot hot. 3. The pot design does not spill or drip when you pour the coffee into the cup. 4. The maker doesn't steam while brewing. I can keep it pushed under my cabinet without worrying about it ruining the bottom of my cabinets. 5. The removable water reservoir means I dont have to store the maker by my sink. 6. It's easy to clean.

I really like this coffee maker. The only thing missing is the programmable feature, but I don't really mind. I can still set everything up and press the button when I arise in the morning. I love the side reservoir, which I didn't think I would like at all, but it's awesome and takes up practically no extra space. It's easy to clean and use, and the best part is that the coffee tastes great. I love the Bold and Small Batch options, too. Also love the cone filter. Unlike some coffee makers I tried, the basket seats securely and doesn't overflow. Overall, a great coffee maker.

review_title: Compact, Quiet, and Still Going Strong After a Year
body_en: This Keurig single-serve coffee maker has been great for everyday use, especially if you don’t want a large machine taking up counter space. I’ve had mine for over a year, use it every day, and it still works just as reliably as it did when I first got it. It brews incredibly quickly, usually in around 30 seconds or less, and it’s surprisingly quiet while running. I also love how small and lightweight it is. It’s easy to move around, pack up, or take somewhere else when needed, so portability is definitely one of its strongest features. I’ve had no issues using different pod options with it. It works with the regular coffee pods I buy, including Starbucks, as well as the reusable pod options I’ve tried. I like having the flexibility to use either prefilled pods or my own coffee without needing separate equipment. Pros: * Excellent space-saving design * Very quiet * Brews in around 30 seconds * Small and lightweight * Extremely portable * Works with multiple pod options * Compatible with reusable pods * Easy to use * Reliable for daily use * Still working great after more than a year Overall: This has proven to be a really dependable little coffee maker. I use it every single day, it takes up barely any room, and I can have coffee ready incredibly quickly. After more than a year of regular use with no issues, I definitely think it’s a great value for the money.

review_title: “Beautiful color, easy setup, and great coffee!” ☕💚
body_en: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Love the color and how easy it is to use! I just received my new Keurig, and I’m really happy with it so far! The dark green color is absolutely beautiful and looks even better in person. It fits perfectly on my coffee station without taking up too much space. Setup was quick and easy right out of the box. Within a few minutes, I had it ready to brew my first cup. I like that it has multiple cup-size options, and it fits my travel mug without any issues. The coffee brews quickly, is nice and hot, and the machine is much quieter than I expected. Overall, it feels well-made and is perfect for anyone who wants a simple, reliable coffee maker without a lot of extra buttons. If you’re looking for a compact Keurig that looks great and makes a good cup of coffee, I would definitely recommend this one!

review_title: Excellent Coffee Maker – Fast, Easy, and Great-Tasting Coffee
body_en: I’ve been using the Keurig K-Express for a while now, and I’m very happy with it. It’s compact, stylish, and fits perfectly on my kitchen counter. The Warm Stone color looks modern and elegant. The coffee brews quickly, and I love the Strong Brew option because it gives my coffee a richer, bolder flavor. The 42 oz water reservoir is convenient since I can make several cups before needing to refill it. It’s incredibly easy to use and clean, making it perfect for busy mornings. If you’re looking for a reliable single-serve coffee maker that delivers great coffee every time, this is an excellent choice. I would definitely recommend it!

First, an introduction, this will take some going through, bear with me. First, I had refused for years to get a Keurig, as I did not feel the quality and richness of a good strong cup of coffee was possible. But I finally got tired of trying other methods of brewing, from using a regular single cup espresso maker, moka pot, pour over, French press... I finally opted for the ease of a Keurig mini-plus. Coffee was ...eh... I switched coffee brands, to what I feel has to be the best commercial brand. And the coffee was EXcellenT! About a year later, despite regular cleaning cycles, the thing just stopped working. I tried to take it apart, watched some youtube videos which just solidified the fact that the company made these non-serviceable. P.O.'d at this obvious tactic to sell more, I waited a few weeks, but went and got another one. Same deal a year later. Another one. This last one gave me signs before ending it's own life. I would have to run several cycles where nothing would come out... till finally something... drip... by drip... several hours later, the thing would start running again, only to stop again the next day or two. Finally, it just died. So I REFUSED to get another. These things are ridiculous, right? So I got a new French press. Coffee is great!! But... omg... what a pain cleaning that thing every.... single... time... I mean, really, it's no big deal. But, it CAn be. So I saw this thing on sale, I thought, well, it's HAlf the price of the other ones... and I def want something different this time. Cut to now.... This thing has SEVERAL issues that I don't like. First of all, it is a thinner cheaper plastic, and has a cheap looking shine to it. Ok, I'm over it. The plastic... I mean, can't they make these things with glass reservoirs.... the plastic reservoir has screws on the inside of it. I don't care if they say it is food safe... Plastic is also considered food safe... but that doesn't mean it is.. those are just bureaucratic rhetoric lies. But I digress,...So this coffee maker has an adjustment for high altitude... is THAT what ruined my previous Keurigs? High altitude? Hmmm. Ok, so maybe that's a plus. It also has different sizes that you can choose -8,10, & 12 oz. With the mini-plus, you choose the size by the amount of water you pour in. That means that this one measures what it sucks in. Hmmm. The mini-plus had the controls on the top. Easy peasy. This one has the controls on the side. It also doesn't have rubber feet on the bottom. So when you try to push the buttons, the thing slides away from you. Impossible to push any buttons with one hand, you have to use two. Even with rubber feet, you have to use two hands. I'm not a paraplegic, but it's rather stupid to have to hold the thing to press a button or two, or three. Which is what you have to do. It's just really awkward because you really have to hold it in the back to keep it from moving when you press the button in front. And you have to do that without touching the reservoir, which will pop out if you tried that. But let's get to the coffee. So with the mini-plus, the first liquid out of the machine, was dark coffee. As it was finishing, the coffee would be a little more clear, but not pure water. With this machine, for the first few seconds, it is spewing out crystal clear WATER. I don't even know how that is possible. But this, it does. It also claims to be faster than the mini-cup. I hestitate to say "brews faster", because it doesn't brew, Keurigs simply spew water into and through the k-cup, it's a pressurized system, not a true brewing system. And it definitely IS faster. And that's a problem, as evidenced by the watery coffee that it spews out. Sure enough, the "coffee" tastes like water. This is the 8 oz brew, mind you, with the machine set to "strong". I first tried the 12oz, and ended up pouring it down the sink. The 8 oz wasn't much better. My next step is to switch out cups while it's pouring out the water at the beginning of the cycle and see if I can get a stronger "brew". All in all, it's convenient enough. But it will sit on my counter, mostly unused, for when I have those really lazy, sleepy, or sick days, when all I want to do is pop in a capsule, and deal with the rest of it... Very disappointed. Perhaps if you live in a low altitude area, the mini-plus would work for you. I really do recommend that one above this.

review_title: Mine did not last a year.

Bought in Oct 2025, and it just stopped working after I cleaned it with descaling solution in June 2026. I had previously cleaned it earlier in the year without any issues. Not sure what went wrong. Not sure if I will buy another one. It was a good thing while it lasted.

I absolutely love my new Keurig K-Express! From the moment I took it out of the box, it was incredibly easy to set up and start using. Within just a few minutes, I was enjoying my first cup of coffee. What impressed me most is how quickly it brews. Mornings are busy, and having a fresh, hot cup of coffee ready in about a minute is a game changer. The Strong Brew button is one of my favorite features because it gives my coffee a richer, bolder flavor without any extra effort. The compact design fits perfectly on my countertop without taking up a lot of space, and the removable water reservoir makes refilling simple. It has been reliable, easy to clean, and consistently brews a great cup every single time. If you're looking for an affordable, dependable single-serve coffee maker that delivers great-tasting coffee and is simple to use, I highly recommend the Keurig K-Express. It has exceeded my expectations, and I couldn't be happier with my purchase!

I got this to replace my original Keurig. The old k50 or whatever it was. This thing takes up less space, looks more sleek, and works better than the original. It's faster, the coffee tastes better, it has the strong button. Also, I keep my coffee maker in my bedroom, and with the old one if you wanted it to be ready to make a quick cup of coffee it had to be turned on which meant that it had lights illuminated. I had to cover them with tape. This new one can go from being turned off to making a quick cup of coffee immediately. And after 5 minutes it automatically turns any illumination off. That means it doesn't make light in my bedroom at night. It's just a way way better version. It's quieter. I love it I'm so glad I got it. I will say that I got this brand new, and it was a really good deal, and I can see why because the manual includes an offer for discounted coffee that expired over two years ago. I'm guessing Keurig punched out a few too many of these models and they've been sitting in a warehouse for too many years. My advice is buy it now before it goes out of stock. It is an excellent coffee maker.

review_title: Practical, economical, and quite good at what it does!
body_en: Neither my husband nor I are coffee drinkers, but we have many family members who are. We had an old Mr. Coffee who should have been called, "Mr. Reliable." Since he was getting on in years, we felt it wise to invest in an economical, low-tech, potential work-horse of a coffee maker primarily for guests and entertaining. Enter Amazon, research, and reviews finally deciding on this model. Now please do not mourn for Mr. Coffee, he is still with us residing in the pantry for emergency service when needed. This particular Hamilton Beach model fit the bill of reasonably priced, low-tech, easy to use and clean, and hardworking from a well established and reliable company. Mr. Hamilton Beach has been in our employ for almost 3 years now, and what an outstanding employee he has been. He has served at multiple parties and family gatherings; he has hosted many, many house guests, and has reliably made coffee when asked to do so. We have no complaints about this faithful servant. The programmable feature, the Select-a-Brew component, the attractive look, and certainly not least of all the delicious coffee others always comment upon when served have all contributed to the enjoyment and functionality of this attractive, unobtrusive coffee maker. The 24 hour preprogramming coupled with the 2 hour shut off give peace of mind whenever it is in use. The swing out basket makes cleaning simple and easy. There have been no malfunctions, leaks, discolorations, or chips or cracks in the carafe. All in all, Mr. Hamilton Beach Programmable Coffee has been a great addition to our kitchen staff! Top 3 Likes: -Reliable, functional, and practical -Easily programmable with safety shut off -Easily loaded and cleaned Top 3 Dislikes: -No Dislikes!

review_title: Don't be afraid to buy this coffee maker. :)
body_en: I regularly read all the negative reviews first to see what the complaints actually are. In many cases, that has kept us from purchasing something of inferior quality. And, of course, sometimes a product is a lemon, so the negative reviews are justified. BUT, many complaints are often very subjective for whatever reason and have little to do with the product's quality or ability to perform properly (i.e., cord is shorter than they like, a button isn't in the right place, it doesn't have this bell or this whistle, etc.). And to be blunt, some folks either don't read and/or understand the product's directions and end up using it improperly, which can damage or shorten it's life-expectancy. Anyway, we ordered this Hamilton Beach coffee maker after reading a boatload of negative AND positive reviews. It worked perfectly out of the box, and, using the SAME coffee we always use, it made a better-tasting brew than the one it replaced (Black and Decker). We just read directions carefully, set it up properly, and made sure we put the carafe where it is supposed to be on the plate so the spring-loaded nozzle actually lines up with the hole in the carafe lid (so there would be no leaks or drips --about which some people complained). No problems. SO...don't be afraid to order this product. It's fine. :)

review_title: Good but has a few quirks
body_en: It brews more slowly than some other brewers. Allow 2 to 4 minutes extra time. The FrontFill feature is nice but you have to nurse water through that front slot. Otherwise you'll get water everywhere. The carafe can weigh if it's close to its capacity. The brewer likes to hold the carafe snugly so keep that in mind when you're removing it. The filter will need a little extra time before it's dry enough to remove. I can't decide if it gets 3 or 4 stars from me so I'll give it the benefit of the doubt. But it does brew a nice cup of joe, I'll admit.

Short and sweet, I just wanted to say that this coffee maker works great. It does have a couple different settings for like "bold" coffee and etc. It keeps the coffee nice and hot. I've had it for quite a while with no problems. I would definitely buy again
l absolutely love this coffee maker. I love the front fill. It makes great tasting coffee and it's just all around great coffee maker!

review_title: short lifespan, bottom-of-the-line features, and -extremely- prone to spilling while brewing
body_en: I used this machine daily for 17 months. Then, quite suddenly, it died: it wouldn't pump water or heat coffee. 17 months is a very short lifespan for a coffee machine. (Another of my Hamilton Beach machines also lasted a little less than 18 months. Perhaps the entire brand suffers from durability issues.) This machine's coffee is as good as the coffee I've had from $50 Hamilton Beach machines. But I regret buying this machine, and indeed, I am never going to buy another Hamilton Beach product. In so many ways, this machine's features are limited or poorly implemented: 1) Extremely prone to spilling coffee all over your countertop. This is not a problem with the carafe; instead, it's a problem with the spring-loaded nozzle that transmits coffee from the machine to the carafe. About once every three months, this Hamilton Beach machine (and others that I've had) floods my countertop. Many other reviewers have detailed this problem: see "Hamilton Beach strikes out again" (which has the best detail), "flow cutoff sucks, leaks", "Coffee Goes All Over the Counter", and more. See also the picture at the bottom of this review. A recommended solution is to use a little less ground coffee than you normally would, and then to use the machine's "bold" setting. But this hasn't stopped my machine from flooding on occasion. This alone is a fatal or near-fatal flaw. But there is more... 2) Water reservoir: not removable (and thus difficult to wash). Also, the water gauge, which lets you see how much water is in the reservoir, appears on only one side of the reservoir -- rather than both sides, as with many other machines. Depending on how you position this machine on your countertop, you may need to bend at an odd angle to see the gauge. 3) Carafe: before making coffee, you push it into the machine so that it sits atop the holder, just as with most other coffee machines. But if you push it in as far as it can go, you have gone too far; the carafe won't be well positioned, and your coffee will spill outside the carafe. (But the carafe itself is better than the carafes from Hamilton Beach machines of a few years ago, because it's less likely to spill when pouring.) 4) LED indicator lights: they're white, which makes it a little more difficult to see whether they're on during the daytime. Any other color would have been better. 5) Power cord: not retractable, as it is on other low-cost coffee machines. As a result, the power cord will spill out over your countertop at least a little. 6) Buttons: they are very shallow and stiff; they require too much force to press. Again, it's not a huge problem. But to press the power button or any other button when the carafe is less than half-full, you need to firmly hold the machine itself with one hand, while pressing the button with a finger of your other hand. If you just attempt to press a button without holding the machine in place or otherwise anchoring it, you'll simply tip the machine over onto its side. 7) Battery backup: there is none. If you lose power for a second, or unplug your machine just for a moment, you will need to reset the current time, the time at which you want coffee-making to start (if you use that feature), and any special settings that you have. This isn't easy, as Hamilton Beach doesn't make it simple for you to set the time or, especially, the time at which you want coffee-making to start. The lack of a backup battery for these features seems like great cheapness on the part of Hamilton Beach, given that ordinary consumers can buy 3V lithium batteries for less than $1. 8) Coffee-filter holder: it has no handle, and to use it, you must slide it into the machine just so. All of this makes it a little difficult to manipulate. 9) As mentioned at the top of this review, the machine died in less than 18 months. This machine is worse than you would hope, even given the low price. And the flooding problem, while it happens to me only once every three months or so, is terrible when it does happen. Avoid Hamilton Beach.

review_title: Great Espresso Quality, but the Portafilter Is Very Hard to Lock In
body_en: I’ve been using this 20-bar espresso machine regularly, and the espresso itself comes out very well. The shots are hot, rich, and flavorful with a nice crema, and the stainless steel body looks great on the countertop. Setup was easy, and the removable water tank makes refilling and cleaning convenient. For its compact size, it does a solid job producing café-style espresso at home. That said, the portafilter is extremely hard to lock into place. It often takes several tries of unscrewing, realigning, and pushing very hard before it finally locks in. At times, I honestly feel like I might break the machine just trying to secure it properly. This is easily the most frustrating part of using the espresso maker and something that definitely needs improvement. The steam milk frother works, but making good frothy milk takes some getting used to. With practice, I’ve been able to get decent foam for lattes and cappuccinos, but it’s not effortless and requires patience to dial in the right technique. Once you get the hang of it, the results are good, just not instant. Overall, this machine makes excellent espresso for the price, and I enjoy using it despite the learning curve. If the portafilter locking mechanism were smoother, this would be an even better experience. Still, for home espresso lovers willing to work through a few quirks, it delivers solid performance.

I was really looking forward to making a cappuccino with this espresso machine. However, as I unpacked it and set it up I noticed a few things. First, before even removing the water tank I saw some large scratches along one side of the tank. The tank was really hard to pull up and out of the back of the machine, so I assumed a prior user might have made the scratches trying to force it out. Then I noticed the 'MAX' waterline label was not visible when the tank is set in the machine; the top of the machine wraps around the tank top so you can't see the waterline label if you're filling the tank that way. Nothing seriously wrong, just annoying. Next, started checking out the milk frother feature. The round knob that adjusts the steam pressure was not great. The movement was not smooth and easy, but got stuck a little bit halfway through turning it. Someone, somewhere decided little rubber suction cups on the bottom was a good idea. I don't think so. Every time you need to move the espresso machine, you get to play tug-of-war with those suction cups. Just plain solid rubber protectors would work better. I put the espresso grounds in the filter, tamped them down and can't wait for my cappuccino. Oh no! I can't push the filter holder (portafilter) into the correct position. I'm pushing really hard now, afraid I might break the machine. After several attempts I gave up. Also, the end of the filter handle was not smooth, it had some jagged edges that inflicted some painful nicks to my fingers. So I never got to try this espresso machine completely. Maybe it would work for you and actually make good espresso. Maybe the design flaws I noticed don't bother you. But from my experience I think I'll pass on this one.

review_title: It takes some muscle to lock in the filter. That's for sure.
body_en: In the box you get the machine, a portafilter handle, a single-shot basket, a double-shot basket, a plastic tamper/scoop, and a small removable drip tray with a splash guard. It has three buttons: single espresso, double espresso, and steam/hot water. The indicator lights stay solid when it’s ready (takes about 45-60 seconds to heat up). There’s also a separate knob on the side to switch between brewing and steaming. First-time setup is straightforward: fill the tank with cool filtered water (I use filtered to slow down scale buildup), run an empty cycle with the portafilter locked in, then run some water through the steam wand to prime the pump. The initial water that comes out is clean, no weird plastic taste. The portafilter locks in from about a 45-degree angle and needs to be pushed in firmly and perfectly straight (or slightly to the right) for the brew to start properly; it can take a little force and fiddling at first. Tamping matters; grounds need to be as level as possible and the rim kept clean, otherwise it won’t seal well. Once it’s locked in, the single and double buttons dispense a fixed volume that produces a decent espresso with visible crema. For milk, the steam wand works fine. You turn the side knob to steam mode, wait for the light, submerge the tip about 1 cm into the milk, and it froths quickly. The wand itself is a simple panarello style. Cleaning it properly is important: the outer plastic sleeve twists off counterclockwise (it’s stiff on purpose), and you really need to remove and rinse both the sleeve and the metal tube underneath after every use, otherwise dried milk builds up inside and affects taste. Overall, it’s a very basic but functional 20-bar pump machine. It makes real espresso and steamed milk in a tiny footprint, requires a bit of care with assembly and cleaning, and definitely rewards a level tamp and a firm hand when locking the portafilter. Nothing fancy, but it does what it’s supposed to do. This review is based on a video transcript. The video can be found on my Amazon storefront/profile.

review_title: Great Features, but Frustrating to Use

Despite following instructions, it kept slipping out until I finally dumped the grinds and started over. I eventually figured it out, but it was not an experience I’d want to repeat with guests waiting for coffee. On paper, this espresso machine offers impressive features — a strong 20-bar pump, temperature control, and a milk frother for cappuccinos and lattes. In practice, though, the challenging design detracts from the overall usability. It’s a sleek, compact unit with potential, but it requires patience and precision to operate smoothly.

I will continue to use this for making the coffee sometimes, since I can get it to work, but I can't honestly recommend that you buy this.

It has a large 40-ounce removable water tank that lasts a while so that’s a great feature. Also, a 20-bar high-pressure pump. It has a pretty good size drip tray. the top is suggested as a cup warmer, but I don’t really see it as that I don’t really feel comfortable putting my cups up there because I don’t want them to slide off. It has a pretty good steam wand to make milk froth and which that functions how it supposed to. It’s a little tricky at first to figure out how to make your drink perfect so it’s all kind of a trial-and-error thing at first. It is about 12 inches in height and 6.7 inches of width. It is a pretty durable machine very low maintenance, and the instructions are pretty easy overall. It’s a nice coffee machine just very basic and perfect for beginners (like me). And a good value. It is not a loud machine, and the temperature of the coffee is pretty hot. You can make a single shot or a double so far, I’ve only made a few mochas, but I still find myself going through the drive-through of a coffee shop lol hard to break old habits but I see myself saving money with this machine also. I recommend this though for beginners and people that want to save money and nice to have at home. On the downside I feel like I have a lot of fingerprints on this so I'm constantly wiping it because I feel like also guest are curious and always want to look at it.

I make two or three drinks a day and fill the tank maybe every four days. The 40.5oz capacity is generous. The drip tray also holds a lot, so I am not emptying it constantly. Less maintenance is exactly what I wanted.

Our office kitchen is tight on space. This machine's footprint is small enough to sit between the sink and the microwave. Colleagues have started using it daily. It's held up well over a few months of shared use.

Been using it for over a week now and so far it's been great, no issues. Came double boxed and well insulated in it's original box inside. Everything comes apart easily to clean. I also used my round percolator paper filters by removing one of the screens, that made the coffee even better by removing even more of the silt ground. Good buy
High quality. Glass is not thin. Looks great. Don't overthink it!
It did its purpose -used for guest.
Wish it was a little thicker but I love this thing. Easy to clean.
Sturdy and durable
It was ok, I did return it though. Not the best quality and smaller thai t thought.
Excellent and very handy stays hot for an hour.
Good press for the price. Would definitely buy again. I do wish the press went all the way to the bottom of the glass, but all in all worth the price.

Was a bit hesitant to buy this one; mixed reviews but I took a gamble. I have not had it very long, but so far I am quite pleased with it. Makes a great cup of coffee. Read your instruction manual before using and abide by it. Three brew settings on the knob: mild, medium, strong. While it's brewing the blue light ring pulsates, then solid blue light when it is finished brewing. Love the color and the style. I also like the fact there is no clock on it so one less thing to reset after a power outage. Simple on/off and nothing to program. Exactly what I wanted.

Great little coffee pot. Brews quickly and tastes great. Wonderful if you are looking for basically 2 regular cups of coffee. This thing is gorgeous as well. The only downside is that it shuts off after 30 minutes and I have to turn it back on. Wish the timer were for 2 hours before auto shut off

review_title: Good little maker for the infrequent coffee drinker
body_en: UPDATE - the Customer service team has gone out of their way to try to resolve the issue. For that they get 2 stars added. Most companies do not care enough to bother. Original review- If you drink your coffee slowly or are only interested in a couple of cups per sitting then it would be better for someone to invest in a pod brewing machine versus this unit. Brews 2 standard coffee mugs per pot. Lasted 8 mos before the 10 minute brew turned to 28 mins and the brew temp went from 142 to 138. Please note the warming plate is on for 1 hour - sometimes. This was fine until that 60 minutes was taken up with 28 mins of brew time. Additionally, the scoops of coffee went from 2 to 3 for the same flavor value. With quality coffee the cost it is now, this is no longer worth the lesser cost of higher end coffee makers. It is cute and if one doesn’t drink a lot of coffee, just needs one to sit on the counter for an occasional guest… this would probably be fine. At minimum, I expected to get a good year of daily use for the price. It started failing about 6 months in. At 8 months the coffee is nearly undrinkable.

review_title: A great little coffee maker and performs faultlessly!
body_en: I love this coffee maker! I have tried so many top of the line, down to the 5 cup Mr. Coffee, and this is a winner! I have owned and used this great little coffee maker for 2-1/2 years. It makes a wonderful cup of coffee. It is a quality coffee maker and I have had zero problems with it since day one. The cost is a little more (or a lot less) than some of the other smaller makes on the market. I am so very happy with this cute little retro looking coffee maker. I own a small Krups, Mr. Coffee and a Cuisinart, and this is the only one that I am 100% satisfied with. The strength adjustment knob does change the strength of the brewed pot. The timing of the finished pot depends on the strength selection, as it slows down the water through the grounds depending on your setting. If it ever stops working, I will be buying another one, as in my opinion, it is the best in its class!

I’ve had my coffee maker 5 months and it’s already broken! It won’t turn on. I use it once or twice per day and follow instructions in the manual. I’ve tried descaling it as the company suggested (that didn't help). Considering this is a $70 coffee maker, I expected it to be good quality. I would love to speak with someone from the company to make this right. It’s a cute style and goes well with my kitchen. I’m a single Mom and can’t afford to buy another coffee maker right now. Can y’all just send me one that works? I feel like everything these days is designed to break (planned obsolescence) so we have to keep rebuying. Please don’t be one of those companies!

review_title: Really read the reviews and seriously consider before buying.
body_en: Definitely not worth $50+. Maybe $25-30?? I'm sure we've all seen the reviews of people who say they received a used item. I didn't and that's not what this review is about. But, if you buy this, buy the paper filters and use those instead of the reusable one until you decide that you're going to keep it. I would return this but the reusable basket is stained and I feel bad returning it used because they would probably just send it to someone else. Some say who cares, but overall the machine is not THAT bad. It has annoying features that are written about in MANY reviews: It's hard to fill up, it leaks out the bottom if you so much as put one, JUST ONE, more drop than the max level, and it super slow on the strongest setting. It's also hard to fill. So I use a 24 oz water bottle. The medium setting isn't too slow. It gives me time to take the dogs out and feed them. So I've learned to use 7 scoops to get the strength I want. But I really wish I had listened to the reviews and bought something else. However, if you're willing to take the chance because you like the way it looks, use the paper filters just in case you decide to return it. It's perfect for me as I'm the only one that drinks coffee in my house. It makes 2 nice 12oz cups. If you don't care returning it used, then it doesn't matter what filter you use. I just don't feel right returning it used and stained...
Very nice

Really cute and compact. Wont' make coffee for a crowd, but perfect for a cup or two. Two wishes...that the lid opened a bit more for pouring the water in, and that replacement carafes were easier to find. This coffee make is so cute and works great. My only complaint is that I wish the warmer stayed on a bit longer. Other than that it is fantastic

review_title: Nearly Eight Years of Service—Good Enough to Buy Again
body_en: I originally purchased the Cuisinart DCC-3200 PerfectTemp 14-Cup Programmable Coffeemaker on October 31, 2018, for $75.92. Nearly eight years later, it still makes excellent, hot coffee. It recently began making a slight squeaking noise during the brewing cycle, so I decided to play it safe and purchase the same model again on August 2, 2026. That should say plenty about how much I like this coffee maker. It is dependable, easy to operate, makes a full 14-cup pot, and has served me well for almost eight years. I would not have bought the exact same model again if the first one had not performed so well. My only complaint is the price increase. The original cost $75.92, while the replacement cost $107.43 before tax—an increase of $31.51, or about 41%. Even with the higher price, its performance and longevity made it worth buying again. Five stars.

review_title: Love it for a consistently good and easy cup of coffee
body_en: Love love love it for a consistently good cup of coffee and so easy! This is our second one of this exact same coffee pot, the previous one lasted about 7 years until it got a crack somewhere and started leaking so the value for the money is definitely there. We debated getting something different this time around but I couldn’t stray from something that we already knew worked great and we never had any issues with. Consistently brews a great flavor and temperature cup of coffee, easy to clean and set up. Would definitely recommend, and the fact that you can set it up the night before and program it to brew is a great feature!

One of the best and cheapest, good looking coffee makers out there. I have one at home and one at the office for years and it works everyday. The coffee is hot, it keeps it fairly hot not burned, easy to fill, easy to add coffee. I have bought many coffee makers and some are much much more expensive. But just for a good consistent pot of coffee once you get the correct measurements of coffee and water I think there is none better. It came with the gold filter which is good since I never use paper, it has a few brew temp and carafe temps and you can set the timer to brew automatically. It does not take up much space is fairly easy to keep clean. The water tank though does take a bit of work to get clean and keep clean though. Over time it gets pretty rank and I cleaned mine by spraying soap and Clorox in it and using a dishrag to clean it out. I then rinsed it out in the sink all the time being upside down so as this would not enter the brew track. Once cleaned and rinsed then filled with water and ran a couple of pots of water through it and its as good as new. Now unless your a professional, I don't recommend doing this LOL but it never stopped working and never stopped brewing a good cup of coffee. Looks and works as good as the day it was purchased. I did buy another one and had a funeral for the old one after many years. It still worked, so it was hard to part with but the wife said we had to get a new one. Sheesh, Why? O well you know how that goes.

I ordered this coffee maker after researching it as thoroughly as possible. Much to my disappointment, the initial batches of coffee tasted like plastic. I ran carafes of filtered water through the device several times, but the taste of plastic persisted. Then I used ChatGPT to see what information was available and sure enough, this is a common problem. It would have been nice if Cuisinart had addressed this issue in the manual. This is why I am giving a 3 star rating. My next step was to use coffee cleaner, followed by 2 more carafes of filtered water. I could still smell the plastic in the filter basket, so I washed it with a strong mixture of Dawn detergent. Then I ran another carafe of water through it. That finally seems to have gotten rid of the plastic taste in brewed coffee. The entire process probably used several gallons of filtered water and took several days to complete. Otherwise, this coffee maker is well designed and of good quality. The plastic components are thick, unlike the current Moccamaster plastic parts which are thin and flimsy by comparison. (The Moccamaster also has a tube attached to the carafe lid that’s unnecessary, cumbersome and hard to wash. Their old models have a separate tube which isn’t used for the same reason.) I desperately needed a replacement coffee maker and I’m glad I persisted in my efforts to get rid of the plastic taste instead of returning it. This makes good coffee as other reviews have stated. Just be prepared to get rid of the plastic taste. UPDATE As of February 7th, I need to revise my rating to 4 stars. Except for the problem with the plastic taste I explained above, this is a high-quality product that makes good coffee. I love the 1 - 4 cup feature which is what I use to make 24 ounces of coffee. If you drink coffee black and enjoy the flavor of good coffee, you will love this feature. This makes the best coffee I've ever tasted. That said, the initial plastic taste with no mention of it in the manual is a major problem that has to be overcome.

UPDATE AFTER USING FOR 6 WEEKS: I've been using this new Cuisinart almost every day for 6 weeks, and have NEVER had any issues with the carafe leaking/spilling OR the condensation on the maker lid leaking water onto my countertop when I open it up to add coffee grounds and pour water into the reservoir. Not even once. The only thing I can think of to explain SOME of those carafe complaints is that they are trying to pour from the carafe TOO fast. I must admit 10 years ago when I FIRST got my old Cuisinart2800, I tried pouring from the carafe and poured too fast and spilled. But just a slight slow down fixed it and no issues since. But other than that pour speed issue, I have no idea what those reviewers were doing to cause the maker or the carafe to leak water as they described. Everything else I wrote in my initial review still stands too! ============================================================= I read thru a LOT of reviews on this Cuisinart DCC3200NAS (this is the SS and Black). I JUST set it up on my countertop last night and ran a pot of plain hot water thru it as suggested. This morning I made my first pot of coffee in it!! 9 cups. Very tasty coffee! BUT this review is NOT about how good the coffee is. Nearly all the reviews have established that its great. This review addresses a few of the most common complaints about this coffee maker. FYI: This new 3200 replaced a refurbed Cuisinart DCC2800WFR I had for 10 years that recently started leaking water. The MOST common complaint is the carafe. I am honestly NOT sure why. The new carafe seems IDENTICAL (except black plastic vs white) to the carafe that was on my 2800 that I used for 10 years with no issues. Spout dripping: The easiest way to MAKE the spout drip is pouring too fast. Just slow your pour down a TICH. I put water for 9 cups in my carafe and poured it into my water reservoir in about 10 seconds without spilling a drop. It works exactly the same way AND as well as my 2800 carafe did for 10 years. No spills. No issues. HELPFUL HINT: Make SURE the 3200 lid is FULLY opened (past 90 degrees) before you try to fill the reservoir. Then just rest the carafe spout on the SIDE of the reservoir with the water level indicator. Pour. Done. Carafe Lid not hinged and/or too tough to take off and/or put back on properly: Not hinged is true! But why is that bad? I don't know. It snaps off and on easily for me. Has for 10 years. And I don't even bother taking the lid off to fill the carafe with water. Just fill it thru the spout hole! The new carafe lid DOES require a SLIGHTLY firmer push to pop it off and back on than my old carafe, but I'm guessing in 12 months this one will pop off and on a little easier than it does now too. HELPFUL HINT: Pop the carafe lid off by LIFTING the tab that your thumb sits on when holding the carafe. Pop it back on in reverse: Insert spout side first, then pop the thumb side down. Done. Easy peasy. The 3200 control panel is significantly different from my old 2800. I read a couple reviews that suggested the 3200 control panel was difficult to understand and use properly!?! I found the exact opposite to be true. Once you know exactly what option each button controls (button labels seem clear & obvious to me), setting the options properly is completely simple. As you press each button, it cycles thru the available settings for that option. Stop pressing that button when that option is set to your liking. If you miss it, cycle around again. Done. The basket the filter sits in DOES need to be PUSHED fully back down such that it "pops" down into the maker after being removed (in my 2800, it just dropped in loosely). BUT that is obvious to the careful user since it requires that same "pop" to remove that basket in the first place. If that basket is NOT popped down into place, the carafe lid won't reach (much less push up on) the spring loaded valve on the underside of that basket, so that valve would stay closed, and as your maker dumps more water into your filter, coffee grounds will overflow your filter and go everywhere including the bottom of the water reservoir. PS: Same thing happens if you put a LIDLESS carafe in the coffee maker! Lid isn't there to push up on the valve, so the valve stays closed. I found the 5 "Coffee is Done" beeps and the 2 "Heating Pad Off" beeps to be the right volume for my house. Not loud, BUT loud enough that on a normal (ie: semi-quiet) morning, I can hear it from the next room easy. AND it is super fast and easy to turn the beeping off and back on with the "Tone" option button if you need to. Bottom Line for me: I am boggled by all the carafe and reservoir filling issues so many reviewers have! I have NO dripping issues or lid issues with my carafe, NO reservoir filling issues, and NO setup or control panel issues. All 5 stars. Now lets just see if it stands the test of time like my 2800 did!

I love this coffee maker. We had this model for at least 5 years. Still worked perfectly but I decided I'd like to buy a new one. I was pleasantly surprised that Cuisinart still makes this coffee maker, the same as previously had, but slightly different buttons etc a bit sleeker, but same functions. It is worth the money. This has been a great coffee maker. Its large capacity is great for when you have company it fits in a small footprint and it keeps the coffee hot! The programming is easy to use and it brews fairly quickly. I am very pleased with it.

This BKSP1 (black stainless appearance) 14-cup coffeemaker replaced a 12+ year old Cuisinart 12-cup unit we used until it finally quit working. Great coffeemaker and it produced great coffee. My research to replace the old unit settled on the BKSP1 model and Amazon delivered straight-a-way. I got it all cleansed out, programmed and set up for begin brewing at 4:45 the next morning. It brewed a great pot of coffee and all worked wonderfully ... EXCEPT that the clock on the BKSP1 was running FAST. It had "gained" almost an hour since I had set it up the day before. Thus the coffee was actually brewed at ~3:45AM. I reset the clock and kept watching it as I would walk by the coffeemaker and noted that it was gaining time or running FAST. I went through this for several days and finally sent a message to Amazon C.S. and they immediately replaced with another BKSP1 and I returned the original unit. I went through the setup process with the #2 BKSP1 and was hopeful that the clock would keep proper time ... however it did not. The clock on the #2 BKSP1 also ran FAST. The coffeemaker worked just fine in all regards ... save for the clock running FAST. So, I reached out to Cuisinart/Conair C.S. with this "fast clock" issue and they replaced the #2 BKSP1 with the #3 BKSP1. I did all the setup with #3 and lo & behold ... the clock on the #3 BKSP1 also runs FAST. All other elements work just fine, brews great coffee, but the clock just has a mind of it's own. So (you can guess what is next), I reached out to Cuisinart/Conair C.S. (again) with the fast clock issue noted in graf above. A ticket was established and I was shipped a #4 BKSP1 to replace the #3 unit. Can you see where this is going? The #4 BKSP1 unit was set up and put into service and the clock on #4 also runs FAST. So ... it appears that there is something common going on with the BKSP1 model units. This time I called Cuisinart/Conair C.S. (I had been establishing all other tickets via the inter-web and e-mail). The lady with C.S. was simply excellent and she noted my BKSP1 ticket history and said she would have another unit shipped out straight-a-way. She asked if I still wanted the same BKSP1 model or would I want to get the SP1 model (SP1 is the brushed stainless appearance). I figured what the heck ... I would get the SP1 this time. In a couple days I received the #5 SP1, got it all set up and ready to brew coffee the next morning at 4:45. I would glance at the clock on the #5 SP1 as I walked by the unit and the clock was ACCURATE. I was again hopeful that the clock would hold and keep proper time. At 4:45AM the brew cycle started and it actually was at 4:45AM. The clock held it's accuracy for one day at that point. It has now been 3-days and the clock on the #5 SP1 is "spot on". So (there is the 'so' word again) I noted on the boxes the coffeemakers were shipped in had the countries of manufacture stamped on them. The BKSP1 units were all manufactured in China. The SP1 unit was manufactured in Indonesia. AHA - I said. There is a manufacturing plant issue going on. I did an extensive observation letter to Cuisinart/Conair about my situation and thoughts of what is going on. BTW - In addition the BKSP1 units all dripped extensive moisture droplets down the back side of the unit when the top lid was opened to removed the coffee grounds. This had me wondering if there was a leak as there was water all over the counter under the BKSP1 units. Turns out the drip lip on the upper back of the BKSP1 appears to be 'flat' without adequate slope to have the water droplets flow back into the reservoir. Also the drip lip is not as deep as what I noticed on the SP1 units. I also observed (on both the BKSP1 and SP1 models) that there is a lot of moisture condensation that collects on the upper front panel where the control buttons are located. To me this could affect the electronics that I'm guessing is located near or behind this panel. Ergo couple items of note for Cuisinart/Conair: 1) Production molds for the BKSP1 and SP1 are NOT the same between the China and Indonesia manufacturing plants. Thus the drip lip issue noted above. 2) The chips/electronics being used in the China plant for the BKSP1 are defective and can't keep proper time. All-in-all ... The Cuisinart 14-cup coffeemaker is an excellent product and works very well and produces great coffee. Save for the units (in my case) that are manufactured in China where the chips/electronics they are using just don't work. Adding to that the manufacturing mold difference that slightly changes the size of the drip lip on the upper back. I would suggest getting the the SP1 model and keep your fingers crossed that it is also manufactured in Indonesia as opposed to China. At least until such time as changes are made in the manufacturing facility in China to correct the noted issues. Cheers, Nolan K.
